subtopic: MUNICIPAL RIGHTS OF MONTREAL AND 'LA PRESSE.'
MUNICIPAL RIGHTS OF MONTREAL AND 'LA PRESSE.'
speechtext:
(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, before the orders of the day are called, I wish to call the attention of the House, and at the same time enter my protest against an editorial published in ' La Presse,' yesterday, February 25, entitled, ' Les Surprises d'un projet de loi,' which states, partly at least, as follows:
The hon. member for St. James, Mtre Hono-re Gervais, has rendered a signal service to the city, in drawing the municipal authorities' attention, before it was too late, on the Bill of the ' Canadian, Liverpool and Western Railway Company ' now before parliament for sanction.
And further:
' La Presse ' has more than once contended that the parliament at Ottawa had no control whatever over the streets of a city, a matter which is altogether under provincial jurisdiction. Montreal has every interest to watch the Bills which are presented either before the provincial legislature, or the federal parliament. Is that done to-day with sufficient diligency?
The city of Montreal could organize, easily and with profit, a vigilance service which is needed to-day. Special agents-most probably these would be lawyers-should reside permanently during sessions either at Ottawa or at Quebec, so that the city could be notified of any measure being presented in which she would have interests of some sort.
But this service should be conducted with the utmost regularity, as a detective agency. We submit the idea to the wisdom of our aldermen; it rests to them now to perfect it and put in operation.
As I have said in the beginning, I think it my duty to protest in my own name and in behalf of my colleagues of the metropolis, who are particularly aimed at in that

editorial, against the false and unjust assertions against the hon. members of this House and of the Railway Committee.
In justice to the promoters of the proposed bill, to the members of the Railway Committee, and particularly to those who in that committee are more directly charged which the interests of the city of Montreal, I must protest against the double injustice of this article.
It is not true, as it is asserted, that the interests of Montreal have been at a particular moment in a serious and imminent danger, that if it had not been for the intervention of the hon. member for St. James, these rights and privileges would have been sacrificed. Every member of the Railway Committee knows what are his rights and duties, and I must immediately state that on the very first time that this bill came before the committee, Tuesday last, the promoters were disposed, in compliance with the request of several members, to add to their bill a clause having for object to safeguard the autonomy, not only of the city of Montreal, but of every municipality through which the company intended to construct its lines and distribute electrical energy.
It was thus entirely unnecessary and supremely unjust to say, as some Montreal papers, and especially ' La Presse,' did say, that the rights of the city of Montreal were in danger.
I protest once more in the name of the members of the committee against the false assertions of ' La Presse ' and other papers in which appeared sensational articles upon this question. I will add only one word as to that part of the editorial of ' La Presse ' where the creation of a vigilance service is suggested. For my part 1 state here that I am opposed to it. As a representative of the city of Monteral I know well enough my duties and the interests of the city of Montreal to dispense with this sort of guardianship to watch over me.
I believe that the interests of Montreal will be well guarded by the hon. members from that city whenever it will be necessary.

House in Committee of Supply.
Post Office-Outside service-Salaries and allowance, $2,737,856.25.
['Certainly.\nSome resolutions reported.\nOn motion of Mr. Fielding, House adjourned at 10.45 p.m.', 'Monday. March 1, 1909.']

There is an increase in this item of $375.47, I shall be ready to give any details that the committee may desire, but I may explain the increase generally. In the post office inspector's division, there is an increase of $10,342.60, made up of the following:-38 increases of $50 each, $1,900;
two increases of $78.25 each, $156.50- one increase of $46; one increase of $40; 11 additional clerkships. These increases are statutory increases.
Will the minister please state who the new appointees were with their offices and salaries?

In the post office in spectors' offices,, we have appointed eleven additional clerks. In the Nova Scotia division, Mr. J. H. Kennedy, junior second-class clerk was transferred from the Auditor General's office to the Halifax post office at a salary of $1,000. In the Ottawa division, Mr. L. E. Johnston, appointed fourth-class clerk at $400, transferred to the London, Ontario, division. E. Stevenson and L. Hamilton Strong, appointed fourth-class clerks at $400 a year each. In the Manitoba division. D. I. Bailey appointed fourth-class at $400. In the Calgary division. T. Humphries was transferred from the post office in Toronto at $1,000, and C. E. Duncan was transferred at $700.
That is, at the same salary as before?

Yes, except that, in the west, we make a special allowance of 15 per cent. We sometimes transfer clerks from the inspectors' offices in the older provinces, because experienced officers are needed for new districts in the west. At present in the west, they have very good staffs. Sometimes, a clerk desires to be transferred from the west to an eastern office, or vice versa. This accounts for these transfers. In the Edmonton division, R. C. Ferguson, senior second-class clerk, transferred from the inside service at $1,100. C. Watson, junior second-class clerk, transferred from Toronto post office at $950. That makes $2,050 for the Edmonton division. In the Vancouver division W. F. Tracey, senior third-class clerk, transferred from junior third-class clerk at $800. A. L. Reid, senior third-class clerk transferred from the railway at $860. a total of $8,010. These represent the salaries of the 11 additional clerks in the inspectors' branches.
What was the total amount of the salary increases? The minister explained the statutory increases and that is all he has explained so far.

I have given the figures for the inspector's office, $10,342. In the railway mail service the figure is $117,553. In the post offices the increase is $247,581.25.

If there are any exceptions to the statutory increases the minister might let us know later.

I know of none. The amount is made up chiefly of statutory increases with the exception of the additional clerkships. I have given my hon. friend particulars of where these additional clerkships have been created. I come now to the additional clerkships. Mr. E. E. J. Evanturel was transferred from the Quebec office to the office of the superintendent of railway mail service in Quebec at $1,200. Mr. H. M. Harris was transferred from the Calgary post office to the office of the superintendent of railway mail service at Calgary at $670. There were nine new appointments at $400 and 75 new appointments at $501 Shall I give the names?

I am not asking for the names. How are the new appointments divided?
for the establishment of a railway mail service. We have two systems, there is a baggage car service and a postal car service. If it is a baggage car, we pay the railway company 4 cents a mile; if it is a postal car, we give the company 8 cents a mile.
What facilities do you get on the baggage car?
A postal car is a post office on wheels, and clerks are stationed in that car to sort and distribute letters, and deliver them at the several stations where the train stops.
I asked what were the accommodations given you on a baggage car for which you pay 4 cents a mile ?
We are supposed to get from the railway companies sufficient accommodation in a special baggage car for our mails, and they are delivered in bags at the stations.

Is there any sorting in
the baggage car?
No, only accommodation for bags. Sometimes the company does the work itself, and has a side service from the station to the nearest post office where the mails are distributed.
Would the minister tell us how many post office inspectors there are in the Dominion?
They are divided between Halifax, Montreal, Quebec, Ottawa and Toronto.
The minister might givi the number in each division.

There is one at Halifax, St. John, Quebec, Montreal, Ottawa, Toronto. London, Winnipeg, North Bay (to be established shortly), Vancouver, Calgary, Moosejaw, Kingston, Saskatoon, Edmonton and Victoria.

In the railway mail service, travelling on postal cars.
What is the necessity for the large increase in number?
The mileage of railways has increased. The moment a railway is built, application is made in the district Mr LEMIEUX.

Would the minister explain what is meant by the inspectors'
offices, on page S-2 of the Auditor General's Report, where $119,000 has been expended?

That includes the salaries paid in that branch throughout the country, and the sixteen inspectors cover the whole district. Let not any hon. gentleman be surprised at the increase in the number of employees in that branch, because the country is expanding, and the moment a new railway is built we are bound to extend the system to that railway.
Would the minister tell us how many men are employed in looking after the rural mail delivery service, outside and inside?

No new employee has been added to the Post Office Department for that branch. We have selected Mr. Ross, of Toronto, the superintendent of post offices in the Dominion, as the chief

organizer of the rural mail system. But we keep the same organization, the same inspector in each district, who will receive petitions, and these are sent to the department at Ottawa. The petitions are sent direct from the people in the country to that inspector, and he will himself advertise, as he does at present, for the opening of new stage routes, and will establish the system himself. We do not need any new employees for the rural mail service So that it will not cost the country one cent more.

I would ask the Postmaster General what treatment he intends to give to the letter carriers in respect to their salaries. I presume it is the intention of the government to give them some increase, and perhaps the hon. gentleman might indicate to what extent? I know that in some places the letter carriers are very hard worked. I do hot know that they get any extra pay for extra work, but
I	do know that for ten days during the last elections, the letter carriers in the city of St. John were kept at work until
II	and 12 o'clock at night, delivering Liberal literature, party literature. I do not know that it was very successful, because when the people were roused out of bed at that unseemly hour of the night and came downstairs to take in letters, and found only some little brochure relating to the Liberal party, they were not filled with thanksgiving towards the Liberal party. That is by the way. But I would like to hear from the minister how he proposes to deal with the letter carriers in so far as their remuneration is concerned.

As regards the extra work which may have been added to the letter carriers, either during the election or at any other time, for instance at the time of the centennial at Quebec, or during the exhibitions in Toronto or Ottawa, of course, they are paid extra. But under no circumstances should the letter carriers be employed for doing one party's work exclusively. He has to distribute the literature of both parties, my hon. friend knows.
I quite understand that.
I do know, from what occurred in my own riding, that my opponent had his address sent down to Ottawa and it was franked back.
By whom?

The initials J. S. F. are used for the frank. I cannot find these initials in the list but such is the case. I find that in many other ridings there are similar cases. By what authority were these addresses franked? There were 6,800 franke l in the county of Dufferin.

I am very glad that my hon. friend called my attention to that fact. I am not responsible for the abuse of the franking system in the House of Commons. That is permitted by law and the post offices in the parliament buildings are under control of the Speakers of both Houses. I have nothing to do with this part of the service. Last year some complaints were made as regards the service in this House. I am glad to be relieved of responsibility for that service by the Speakers of both Houses and the committee on internal economy. But, nobody has the right to so misuse his frank as to send for outside parties, literature, letters or parcels. Members, I know, as a rule, confine themselves to their own mail, but my attention has been called this year by one firm in Toronto to the fact that envelopes containing circulars were coming from the House of Commons under the franking privilege. I could not believe my eyes, but I was unable to ascertain whose initials they were. Again, I may tell hon. members who are new in this House that the franking privelige is strictly confined to the members of the House and that it is therefore personal to them only.
After ten days have elapsed members of the house have no authority to frank.
No.

Surely the Postmaster General does not pretend to divest himself of responsibility and to throw the whole blame on the Speakers of the two Houses? It is a notorious fact that what I have described occurred. In my own riding 6,800 of these addresses were received by the electors. I received one t myself. Therefore, I think that the hon. gentleman must hold himself responsible for that state of affairs. This is only one of the many other cases. Yet, no Conservative could avail himself of that privilege. Not only was ordinary literature transmitted, but here was the address of my opponent sent from this House and franked with the initials J. F. S. This is a palpable abuse. It occurred some ten days before the election and three days before the nomination. These addresses were sent around broadcast and not only that but the electors got tons and tons of literature. That is not British fair play. It is the reverse, and the Postmaster General cannot throw the burden upon some one else. He is responsible for it, he is at the head of the department, and if the Speakers of the House have allowed that to take place, I think there should be an investigation. I do not think it is quite fair that literature should be sent in that way from this House when the Conservative candidates had not the same privilege. Here is a concrete case

that should receive the attention of the minister.
It might happen that as last session was well known to be the last session of the parliament a good deal of mail matter might have accumulated.
No one knew that but the hon. minister.
I do not know; it may not be true.
No, but the minister knew that it was the last session.

The post office in the House of Commons is not under my control. It is under the control of the Speaker. I do not appoint a man in the post office. I have no authority over the officials in the House of Commons post office, but I was assuming that if literature was sent to my hon. friend's riding after the session was over it might have accumulated here with other literature. At all events I do not wish to condone the action of the owner of the cabalistic letters J. S. F. The initials ' J.F.S.,' had no success in Dufferin. My hon. friend has been returned and we are all pleased to see him here.

If the literature had borne fruit as they expected it would there might have been a different result. But my hon. friend says it might have accumulate. No, the time has passed for that; my opponent was not in the field, he had not issued his addressi and therefore it would have been utterly impossible for him to have sent it down here in time to have it franked during the session and sent back.
I care not who is responsible, whether it is the Speaker or not ; he ought to be brought before the bar of this House and we should know whether that state of affairs is going to continue.

My experience in the late election was somewhat like that of my hon. friend from Dufferin (Mr. Barr). My opponent used the mails very freely and used the frank of some person whose frank is recognized in the House of Commons post office. The county of Halton was flooded with campaign literature having stamped upon it the 'Compliments of Dr. W. S. Harrison.'
That was your opponent?

That was my opponent. These envelopes, as the minister will observe from one I have caused to be laid on his desk, were passed through the House of Commons post office and franked by some one whose initials look like B. F. C. Who is B. F. C.?
The Minister of Customs.

No, I think it is not the Minister of Customs nor yet is it the Postmaster General, but I believe there is no doubt that it is some one in the service of the government. We know that between sessions no member of parliament has the right to frank literature. The moment the gun fires, or, at any rate within a few days afterwards, the right of every member of the House to use the frank ceases and he is unable again to use his frank until he has been returned and within ten days again of the opening of the next session. I think it very peculiar that a gentleman who had never been in the House of Commons, who had never represented the county, should have a privilege from the government that was denied me. I did not have the privilege of franking letters at that time because this all took place between two sessions of parliament. These envelopes reached my county about ten days before the election and were circulated in very large numbers. The postage would be six cents each on these letters, or $60 a thousand, and there being 5,000 electors in my county the post office revenue has been robbed of at least $300 in that one county. I do not accuse the Postmaster General of having any guilty knowledge of this, nor do I accuse any officer in his department, for I think they are too careful of their duties to do such a thing. But no doubt there is some person in the employ of the government whose frank is recognized by the postmaster in the House of Commons and who either used this frank or permitted it to be used for the benefit of Dr. W. S. Harrison, my opponent. I am not complaining about the character of the literature sent out; it was very tame; it did not amount to much. One portion of it was intended as a tirade of abuse upon the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), but that hon. gentleman is held in so high esteem in Halton that it had no injurious effect on him and it certainly did not hurt me. Some more of that literature had reference to the prosperity of Canada under Liberal rule.
Hear, hear.

Well, the people of Halton had been reading the newspapers and they understood more about the prosperity of Canada than they could learn from this literature which was sent out in a fraudulent way a week before the election. Dr. Harrison had a perfect right to circulate campaign literature in the county of Halton, but he had no right to circulate it at the expense of the country, because it was fraudulent, it was robbing the revenue of the country, it was pure graft. As I told the people in Halton, the very fact that a man seeking their support should come before them in such a manner, grafting and dredging the treasury, to endeavour fo secure his election; well, is it any won-

der that the people would not give their confidence to a man who would be party to such a thing. I most strenuously complain that any officer of the government should be permitted to do such an act. I do not ask that that official be dismissed, for that might be too harsh treatment and perhaps he did it in his zeal for the cause in which he felt a warm interest, but he certainly ought to receive such a strong rebuke as would deter him and others from doing that kind of thing in future. The Postmaster General, if he takes the Civil Service list, will be able to trace out who the guilty party is, and I think it is his duty to do so. I am quite sure there was no authority in law for this.

Hear, hear.
. Mr. HENDERSON. I am glad the minister assents to that.
Hear, hear.

I produced these envelopes in the county to show how my opponent was dredging the treasury, and I stated that I would draw the attention of the Postmaster General to it in the House of Commons, so that he might take steps to protect the revenue of the country. In every shop in every village throughout the country there were a number of these envelopes to be found in the waste paper baskets, showing that the people paid very little attention to the literature. But the point I make is that the revenue was robbed and that some measures ought to be taken to prevent its recurrence in the future.
I don't want the hon. member for Halton to attribute any blame to the postmaster of the House of Commons.
I did not do so.
If the hon gentleman looks at the envelopes he will find they were mailed at the city post office and not in the House of Commons post office.
Is there a frank on it?

There is a frank on it and the Postmaster General knows who it is. Now, this being mailed from the city post office who else than the minister has the right to frank a letter from that post office? As I understand it, it is only the minister and his secretary who can frank at that post office, and it is the duty of the Postmaster General to go to the city post office and ask why the official there allowed this mail matter to go out without this frank.

I corroborate what has been said by my hon. friends. The Liberal literature circulated throughout my county was mailed at the city post office and the
initials used for the frank were very difficult to decipher. I took one of these envelopes to the city post office and the official there told me he knew the frank and that it was perfectly good, but he did not tell me the name. These envelopes containing Liberal campaign literature were circulated all over my county, and inside was a typewritten slip bearing the legend:	'with the compliments of P. R.
McGibbon.' This gentleman never was a member of the House of Commons, but nevertheless he was able to use this frank to send out his literature to appeal to the electors to vote against me.

If the Postmaster General will look at the envelope he will find that it was franked with the initials only, and not the full name of the person who franked through the mails. Liberal campaign literature was similarly circulated throughout my county and my opponent, who was a very decent fellow, admitted at the nomination that he was asked from Ottawa to send down anything he wished to have franked through the mails and he regretted very much that he had done so. He said he did not understand the state of affairs or he would not have allowed this mail matter to go through the post office in a surreptitious way. The fact is now clear that these envelopes were not sent through the city post office, and so the Postmaster General himself must assume the responsibility. I do not blame the Postmaster General. I know that he is a man far above doing such a thing, knowing that it is contrary to the law. But it is up to him to investigate this matter and to let us know who is the culprit, and then punish him for what he has done.

My attention has been drawn to the fact that I made a mistake in reading the name of the post office on these envelopes. In examining the envelope more closely, I find that the stamp is the Ottawa post office instead of the House of Commons post office; so that the matter would come within the duties of the Postmaster General. I make this correction, because I do not wish to impute anything improper to the postmaster of the House of Commons.
I am informed by the deputy that this was sent through the Ottawa post office, and not through the House of Commons post office, and therefore I must say that it was wrong.
What are the initials?
The initials are not very plain.
Here is one on which the initials are very plain-"R. F. C."

I am informed by the deputy that when there is an accumulation of mail matter at the House of Commons, it is usual, in order to expedite its transmission, to send it direct in bags to the Ottawa post, where it is stamped. My hon. friend from Leeds (Mr. Geo. Taylor) will remember that during the session of 1904 the corridors of the House were simply jammed with literature which was being sent out by both sides of the House, as we all expected the elections, and it took several weeks after the session to get that literature sent. We had to provide special cars for it. and it is onlv just to my predecessor, Sir Wm. Mulock. to say that he offered every facility to my hon. friend from Leeds to expedite the sending out of that mail matter.
Tons of it were never delivered.

I do not! think that is the testimony of the hon. member for Leeds. At all events, let me state my own case, and the House can judge from it. Of course, the frank of the Postmaster General is accepted at any post office, wherever he may be. However, during the last campaign I was not in Ottawa, but in Quebec, and I paid the postage at the Quebec post office on each letter and each circular I sent out. and gave instructions to my secretary to see that that was done. Of course, the ministers enjoy the privilege, while in office, of franking their own mail matter.
Can they extend the privilege to others?

I must say that they must not, and, speaking for myself, I would not. The franking privilege of members of the House of Commons is in the same position. Members of the House of Commons must not abuse' that privilege.
I think we ought to have a promise from the minister before we pass this item that he will investigate this matter.

Certainly. Notwithstanding what the hon. member from Leeds has stated, I certainly could not say what are the initials on this envelope. At all events, these initials at that date, and the stamn of the Ottawa post office on the envelope make the matter look rather suspicious, and I will have it investigated. Certainly, subject to the explanation I have just given I would not approve of it.
What are the initials of the deputy Postmaster! General?
"R. M. C."-Robert Miller Coulter. These are not his initials.
Will the Hon. Postmaster General read the law on the subject?

Sections 75 and 76 of the Post Office Act are as follows:
75.	All letters and other mailable matter addressed to or sent by the Governor General, or sent to or by any department of the government, at the seat of government, shall be free of Canadian postage under such regulations as are, from time to time, made in that respect by the Governor in Council.
76.	Letters and other mailable matter addressed to or sent by the Speaker or Clerk of the Senate or of the House of Commons at the seat of government shall be free of Canadian postage, and letters and other mailable matter addressed to or toy any member of either House at the seat of government, during any session of parliament, or to any of the members at the seat of government as aforesaid, during the ten days next before the meeting of parliament, shall be free of Canadian postage.
According to that, the minister would have no right to frank anything except matter on the business of the department?
Yes, the official business of the minister.
Then, I would ask the minister what he would say if a minister of the Crown franked out during election time matter for other people?
I would not do it myself;
What would the minister say and do under these conditions ? Because I think I have in my office an envelope that was franked and used for this purpose.
In such a case, I would severely reprimand the minister.
The Postmaster General (Mr. Lemieux) referred to the fact that in the session of 1904, preceding the election, the whip of the Conservative party franked out a large amount of literature

If my hon. friend (Mr*. Geo, Taylor) will allow me. I did not wish to find fault with that; he was acting with-* in his right in franking that literature out during session. But I said that the whips of both parties had franked a great deal of literature, and there was a large accumulation of it, as the hon. gentleman remembers, in the corridors of this House. That literature was sent out long after the session was over. What I said was in explanation of this case.
The minister does not mean to suggest that these envelopes of which we have spoken were franked and mailed in this House during last session ?

I did not say that.
Mr. PERLEY, But that is the suggestion. The hon. gentleman referred to four years ago This case has nothing to do with four

years ago, because these envelopes had in them typewritten slips which were marked as coming with the compliments of candidates of the Liberal party who were not nominated until weeks after the session was over. Why should the Postmaster General refer to the case of four years ago, and try to make the suggestion that possibly these envelopes were posted in this House last session, when he knows that that could not have been the case?

I am glad the Postmaster General has referred to this case of four years ago, and has quoted the law, and stated that I was within my rights in franking out literature during the session. But he will remember the discussion that took place in the press, and he will remember that every Grit paper in the country hounded me as a violator of the Independence of Parliament Act for having franked out this literature.
It did not hurt my hon. friend (Mr. Taylor). He is still here, and as young as ever.

The Postmaster General of that day, knowing that we were sending out literature, refused to have it sent down to the post office. That is why it remained here to block the corridor-it was simply to deprive us of the opportunity to get our literature out. The hon. gentleman said that I remained here after the session until it was gone. Nothing of the kind; I went home as soon as the session was over. The literature was sent down to the post office and was ultimately sent out, but even then, in many of the post offices throughout the country it was not delivered. But the case we are now discussing is a different case entirely. This matter was not mailed during the session under the frank of a member of parliament. As ha3 been pointed out, it was sent out with the compliments of men who were not nominated until long after the House was prorogued, and it was mailed at the city post office and not at this House of Commons. I have no doubt that the work of addressing this literature was done by civil servants and paid out of the public money. The Postmaster General should ascertain who franked this matter and should make them restore to the treasury the money thus unjustly taken. Unless the Postmaster General does this, he will not be discharging his duty faithfully. I am sure he knows whose frank is admitted to the post office.
Will the hon. gentleman say what initials were used ?

The Postmaster General must know whose frank it is. If not, then the postmaster at the city post office will know. The postmaster here can inform the Postmaster General why he accepted that stuff, and sent it out at the country's expense. He certainly would not do that except on an order approved by the Postmaster General or his deputy.

I assure my hon. friend (Mr. Geo. Taylor) that, since I have been Postmaster General, no officer of the department has been authorized to take upon himself to let any political mail matter pass free through the Ottawa post office to please the party. I would not do it myself, and I would not allow my subordinates to do it. I challenge my hon. friend to name one single instance where this has been done by the post office authorities.
Hon. members here to-day have stated that this material has gone through.
I cannot distinguish the initials of the frank, nor can my hon. friend. I have stated that I will investigate this case. But I cannot make out the initials.
Then, better let the item stand until the minister makes the investigation and is ready to report to the committee.
I will investigate.

I say that this is the most outrageous case that ever took place in this House since I became a member of it. And yet I have had to take abuse for doing that which the Postmaster General himself admits was within my rights. But I do not mind, for the more abuse I get, the more my majority increases. I think it is the duty of the Postmaster General, in the interests of the country, to ascertain who is at fault in this matter.
I will. .

As our Ontario friends have called attention to this matter, I would like to have the Postmaster General understand that Ontario is no exception. The province from which I come was flooded with this stuff. In my own county, three days before the election, this stuff was delivered in thousands of copies through the post offices. I attribute my success in the county largely to this literature, therefore, I am not going to protest against it. But it is an outrage that a private individual, one not a member of this House, should be allowed to frank material through the mail out of session and within a few days of election. I hope there will be an investigation, and, if it is proven that this was done without authority, that the parties responsible will be punished. I may say that the Conservative organizer in Winnipeg had dozens of these envelopes brought to him.
Without postage ?
Yes, and the initials on the envelopes I make out to be ' B F C.'
Is the franking of unofficial matter an offence punishable under the Act ?	-

We have never made it a penalty. We have always thought that those enjoying the privilege would remain strictly within the privilege. But I am afraid we shall have to take severe measures if these are not forged names. Of course, a forgery comes under the criminal law.

I can tell the minister of a case in which, there is no difficulty in recognizing the name used. I have seen literature circulated in my riding, in session and out of session during the past two years, campaign literature of the Liberal party, and bearing the frank just as distinct as the address upon the letter,
' J. B., Sol. Gen.' I am sorry the Solicitor General (Mr. Bureau) has just left the Chamber. I wished to speak about this matter when he was present. After the session the frank is changed, so that it is evidently not a mere oversight, and the person sending it recognizes that the sessional frank does not carry in the recess. All through the recess the weekly circular letter of the Liberal party goes out in printed envelopes addressed to the Liberal press of this country and bearing the frank ' J. B., Solicitor General.' There is a clearly defined case on which the Postmaster General may work.

I would not condone any abuse of the franking privilege by even the Solicitor General, but I may frankly say that it happens sometimes that I send to some of my friends speeches delivered by the Minister of Finance or by the Minister of Customs. The Finance Minister may deliver a speech on the financial condition of the country which I judge should be read by some of my electors, and I would not consider it an abuse of privilege to send such a speech under my frank It is my official correspondence with the people in my county.
We are not discussing that.

If the Solicitor General sends clippings to twenty-five or thirty papers in British Columbia each week, I would not consider that as an abuse. I do not know if the statement is true, although I do not challenge my hon. friend's assertion. The Solicitor General has entered the Chamber and is now in his seat and he will explain himself. I was Solicitor General myself and inquired if I was on the same footing as the ministers. I do not consider that an abuse. To send out tons of literature might be an abuse but to distribute twenty or sixty circulars to newspapers explaining the policy of the Liberal party does not appear to me an abuse.

It may be because I am only a tyro in parliamentary affairs but I cannot subscribe to the doctrine of the Postmaster General. When this matter came to my attention I regarded it as an aggravated instance of petty graft, about as bad as any graft I had observed. As the Solicitor General is now in his seat, I shall repeat what I said, that during the past two years, in session and out of session, the weekly circular letter of the Liberal party, a letter devoted to the most scurrilous abuse of the Conservative party and its leaders.
That is a matter of opinion.

That is a matter of opinion, as the hon. gentleman says, and it is my opinion, and I have a right to state my opinion. This letter, devoted to scurrilous abuse of this side, goes out during session and during recess, bearing the frank of ' J. B., Solicitor General.' The letter is in print. It is not got up by the Solicitor General himself, or representing the product of his literary talents, but is a circular prepared outside, and printed outside as far as we can see and must be carried into the department. Every week 200 or 300 of them are sent out, all with that frank, and to my mind, 200 or 300 offences are thus committed each week against the postal laws to save the paltry sum of $3, which would carry these circulars through the mail. The reason thi3 seems an aggravated and a contemptible piece of graft, is that if the post office officials catch a private citizen in the unintentional act of putting a small piece of paper in a newspaper, they hale him before a magistrate and mulct him. Who would direct this prosecution ? Yet we find the Solicitor General, who would prosecute a private citizen, committing 300 offences every week and the Postmaster General saying that because this is party warfare, he sees no offence in it. I do not subscribe to that doctrine and feel that the House will not subscribe to any doctrine so monstrous as that.

I have no apology to make. I am not surprised at the harangue of my over scrupulous friend from New Westminster. I heard him insinuate the other night that I was in collusion in letting out Bill Miner. I claim that in franking this literature there was no crime and no offence.
Was it no crime to let out Bill Miner?
I do not know but my friend had something to do with Bill Miner.
Order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That expression would not be in order.

I take it back, I do not want to Connect my friend with Bill Miner;
I will let him connect others. I did not misuse the post office for any purpose. That literature notwithstanding the judgment of the hon. member for New Westminister fMr. J. D. Taylor) is sound literature. I have read some of it, and I think it contains sound principles, and if the people of British Columbia had followed it more closely they would be better off to-day than they are.

I would like to inform the Postmaster General of what took place in the district of Nipissing. Tons of this stuff were sent out franked in that way. The distribution was so general that even the Conservative candidate got a copy.
What frank was it?

I have not got any with me now, but I can get some. Tons of that stuff was sent there franked, and went through the mails. Now the hon. gentleman from Halton (Mr. Henderson) figured out a little while ago that the loss to the Post Office Department was something over $300 in his constituency alone. Taking the 221 constituencies in the Dominion of Canada, you have a loss of $66,000 in the revenue of the Post Office Department. Now, if a man wipes the mark off a postage stamp and the country only loses 2 cents by it, he very soon finds himself before a police magistrate and receives severe sentence. I think the Postmaster General will not be doing his duty if he does not institute at once a thorough investigation into this whole matter, and see that the law is carried out according to what he read a little while ago. I think this is one of the most scandalous and disgraceful acts that could be perpetrated upon any people; and if he will investigate this outrage he will not only please the people of Canada, but please the majority of the members on his own side.

So far as my constituency is concerned, I did not see one piece of literature franked by any Liberal during the whole campaign, or any kind of franked literature. The hon. gentleman says there was a loss of $66,000 throughout the whole Dominion by this means. Well, if you have a loss of $66,000 through the use of franked literature, and still have a surplus of $1,500,000 or $2,000,000 to what an extent must the Conservatives have used the franking privilege in their time when they had a deficit every year of half a million dollars?

I hope the minister will not only investigate this subject himself, but that the Public Accounts Committee will bring before it some of these men and make a thorough investigation. The western part of the province of Ontario was flooded with this literature, practically every riding. I was in a great number of 53
ridings myself, and everywhere I found the ridings flooded with this literature, franked from Ottawa, tons of it. Listening to the statement of the minister with regard to the position that the Post Office Department in the House of Commons was in shortly after the close of the session, I could not help thinking that at least some, person in his department was well aware that this literature was being sent out after the 16th of September, because I have a piece of literature in my hand, explaining the wonderful boon of the rural free mail delivery which the minister promised to the people of Canada. This was sent into my riding.
Sent from the Post Office Department? Is it a general pamphlet?
Y'es, a general pamphlet under the same stamp as mentioned by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain).
Does the hon. gentleman mean that it was sent from the Post Office Department at Ottawa?

I cannot help thinking that some one in the Post Office Department had something to do with placing in the literature ' Free rural mail delivery of Canada.' giving the explanation of it that the minister did in that wonderful speech of his at Niagara. This may not be an occasion to pursue the matter further, but I sincerely hope that I shall be given an opportunity to explain what I think the position of the minister was in regard to the stand he took on that occasion.

I have here a postal card which was mailed to the leader of the opposition at Halifax, delivered there through the mails, and I would like to submit it to the Postmaster General. _It bears no frank at all, but it bears the Halifax-Campbell-ton stamp. I gather from that that the postal card was mailed on the train, and that the postal mail clerk was in collusion with the party whose ends were to be served. You will notice that it depicts the right hon. the leader of the government endeavouring to pull the hind leg off a horse, and on the front of it, in red type, it asks the people to support Mr. Reid and the greater Campbellton. This is not a more flagrant boast of a right to hold in contempt the legislation with regard to the Post Office Department than that offered by the Solicitor General. If the Postmaster General properly read the law a few moments ago, sections 75 and 76 of the Post Office Act, then I submit that the Solicitor General was guilty of a breach of that Act. If, in making his admission before this House he had exhibited any extenuating circumstances, or had shown that he repented or was sorry for what he had done, we could have some consideration for him; but he could not in a more flagrant way have exhibited his utter indifference and disregard



of one of the most important laws on our statute-books.
Prosecute him for a breach of the laws.

Would the hon. gentleman pardon me for interrupting him? I do not wish to unload my sins on any other man's shoulders, but I wish to remind my hon. friend that post offices and customs houses, all public buildings, are under the charge of the Public Works Department and not under mine. Every public building is under the Minister of Public Works.

Then I will not read any further from the letter. The Minister of Public Works may take cognizance of it. I will bring this aspect of the matter up at some other time because I have no desire to embarrass the Postmaster General with matters that do not come within his jurisdiction. But, I would like to emphasize the fact that the reading of the Post Office Act a few minutes ago by the Postmaster General is enough, on the voluntary admission of the Solicitor General, to show that he has violated that Act.

I want the hon. gentleman (Mr. Maddin) to correct that statement. I never admitted that I violated the Act; I said that I had not violated the Act. I do not want it to go upon 'Hansard ' that I admitted that I hail violated the Act.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: A declaration by an hon. member as to what he said must be accepted.
I have no desire to misquote the hon. gentleman. I will put it this way.
I want the hon. gentleman to take that back.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Maddin) is stating it within order. I presume that is his intention.

Yes, Mr. Chairman, that is my intention. I submit that on the admission of facts voluntarily made by the Solicitor General he has been guilty of an infringement of this Act, and that it is the duty of the Postmaster General to institute a prosecution against him.
I never made that statement. I say I am not guilty of an infringement or of a violation of the Act, that I kept within the Act.
I said that upon your admission of the facts-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not understand the hon. member for South Cape Breton to be charging that the Solicitor General admitted a breach of the Act. I understand him to be stating that the facts that the Solicitor General mentioned con-situte a breach of the Act in his opinion.

Exactly. That is all I do say and that is all I wish to convey. I submit that upon his admission of facts here this afternoon it becomes the duty of the Postmaster General, who is the special guardian of this piece of legislation, to see that it is lived up to.

As regards that post card, it might happen that when post cards and ordinary envelopes are stamped some may escape the attention of the postmaster. During elections especially, ,or at any time, when there is a large mailing process going on it may happen that the stamp is forgotten upon one envelope. In the large offices in Halifax, Montreal, Ottawa, Toronto and Winnipeg, there are machines run by electricity for stamping envelopes and the absence of stamps sometimes escapes the attention of the stamper. In this case I have no hesitation in saying that if the postal card was knowingly mailed without a stamp, not only the sender but the stamper who passed it was guilty of an offence. I do not wish to justify the action of any guilty party but it quite often happens in ordinary business that a man may fail to detect the absence of a stamp on a letter or card. The very fact of sending an unstamped card to the leader of the opposition on a political question shows, it seems to me, that the sender could not have been acting in bad faith, and that it was a mistake. I would not defend a guilty act.

I am very glad to hear the Postmaster General say that he .does not think that a minister of the Crown has a right to frank out, during recess, election literature for the benefit of candidates who are put forward by the Liberal party. I have obtained the envelope that I referred to. It is addressed to Mr. Murdoch McRae, Harrington East, Que.
It contains a speech delivered by Mr. E. M. Macdonald, M. P., Pictou, N. S., and inside there is a typewritten slip with the ' compliments of P. R. McGibbon.' It was mailed at the city post office on the 30th September and marked ' free.' I took it to the city post office and asked about the frank which seems to be in blue pencil, and they told me that it was ' S.A.F., M. A.' I am glad to see that the Minister of Agriculture is here, and I believe that it must be his frank. I would like, under these circumstances, to ask the Postmaster General to reprimand the Minister of Agriculture right here now, while we are all present.
Would the Minister of Agriculture be good enough to say whether it is his frank or not.
I cannot say whether it is, but it is quite possible.

I can only add the evidence afforded by what has taken place in my riding to what has already been said by many hon. members on this side of the House. I do not at all object) to a member using his franking privilege himself and perhaps overstepping the mark a little, but I certainly object to any person using the frank which is the special privilege of members of this House and of Cabinet Ministers. I think we have proof that somebody has been using a frank which he has no right to. We must not forget that we on this side of the House represent more than forty-five per cent of the electors of Canada, and I say it is not right for the government, or any one on behalf of the government, to use the special machinery of the government for the purpose of distributing campaign literature to the injury of forty-five per cent of the people. We have a concrete case of somebody having made use of the stamp which is the special privilege of a member of this House, and having passed the matter through the post office. There is no doubt that tons of that literature have been passed through the post office with that frank upon it, and the postmaster should have known that it bore the frank of somebody who was not entitled to use it. I want to ask the Postmaster General what he is going to do with the person who absolutely and without authority uses that stamp for the purpose of transmitting tons of literature through the mails, as has been done during the past year? I have noticed that 53J
it is a favourite way for ministers to dispose of a question by saying, ' I will inquire into it,' and then the interest drops, but, assuming that it is proved that this gentleman has used that frank without authority, what is the Postmaster General going to do? Is he simply going to administer a severe reprimand? If that is all he is going to do anybody will be justified in using the frank. If the Post Office Act does not provide some penalty for a man who unjustly uses the franking privilege it is high time that an amendment was brought in to make it a criminal offence for any person to use the franking privilege who has no authority to do so.
I may say at once that the supposed franks which have been exhibited this afternoon reveal a state of things which I will not tolerate.
Hear, hear.

I have no hesitation in saying that the envelope just produced by my hon. friend (Mr. Perley) dees not bear the initials of the Minister of Agriculture.
I know the initials of the Minister of Agriculture.
What are they?
He admits it is his frank.

Oh no, he does not. My hon. friend insinuated a moment ago that the initials B.F.C. were the initials of a member of the government, but that is not clear to my mind. At all events I say that this state of things cannot be tolerated because the Post Office Department must have the respect of all parties in the country, and I intend for the future to see that the spirit and the letter of the law shall be carried out.
Hear, hear.

In the past we may have been a little lax in framing regulations, trusting that those who enjoy the franking privilege would use it prudently and not indiscriminately. We will frame such regulations as in the future only purely official business bearing the frank of ministers and members of parliament will go through the mails. I may say that since the beginning of the session I have received complaints from certain firms in reference to the abuse of the franking privilege. I attribute the reason for these complaints to the fact that it was done by new members of the House.

Does the Postmaster General mean to interpret the Act so as to prevent a member of parliament from franking any mailable matter unless it is of a business character?
1C71

A member of the House has a right to frank all his business letters -I mean business letters in connection with the. public business of the country. But, the other day I received from a firm in Toronto an envelope bearing the frank of one of the new-members of this House who sent.broadcast through'the country circulars inviting the public at large to subscribe to shares in a certain mine in the Gowganda district. That was clearly an abuse of the privilege. The franking privilege is given to enable a member to correspond with his Constituents, and with his family, and with the public generally on public affairs, but it is not given to enable a member to send thousands and thousands of circulars inviting persons to take shares in a mine. That is an abuse of the privilege. It seems to me it it is a mere matter of common sense.
Mr: CARVELL. Now that the Postmaster General has so clearly defined his view of the law and the attitude he intends to assume in the future, it seems to me there is one very important omission, because the Postmaster General has not stated the punishment he intends to mete out to the culprit who franks these documents in this way. I would imagine from the evidence given by so many hon. gentlemen opposite that there must have been a large number of these documents sent to different parts of Canada, and some punishment should be dealt out to the culprit. I would suggest to the Postmaster General that if in the first place he can find out who the official is, he should send him to the Bishop of British Columbia and get him to make a confession and I have no doubt the bishop would treat it as an absolute secret, and his name will not become public, and I dare say the bishop would very kindly assure us that there is no polities in it, and possibly His Lordship would be willing to absolve even the Solicitor General.

With regard to the franking privilege. I quote from the Post Office regulations, page 21, which, referring to the Cabinet Ministers says:
All letters and other mailable matter from the public departments at Ottawa and franked as being of an official character.
That is the only right the ministers have to frank, and when the Solicitor General says he had a perfect right to do what he has done, I am not surprised at the interpretation of the law which we sometimes get from the Justice Department of Canada. The Postmaster General says that the private member of parliament has only the right to frank letters on the business of the country, but the regulation does not say that; it says:
Letters and other mailable matter addressed to or by any member of the Senate or of Mr. SPROULE.
the House of Commons whether on public business or on the personal affairs of such member.	.
That shows the interpretation of the law is broader in the case of a member of parliament than it is in the ease of a minister.
What is meant by 'personal affairs.' ?

I presume it is his own personal business. I do not know anything about the instance the Postmaster General has referred to, but if that member of parliament were engaged in mining it would be his personal business to send out these circulars, and the regulations would appear to justify him in that.

I will take my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) as my witness. Taking the regulations which he has just read and assuming that letters written to his family or to his constituents or to the public on public questions constitute his personal business as the word ' personal ' is generally understood, now would the hon. gentleman take it upon himself to send broadcast thousands and thousands of circulais under his frank, asking the public to subscribe to shares in a mine? He would not
I would not.
He would not, and every one knows he would not do it, and in not doing it he would be guided by his own conscience, his own sense of honour, and common sense.

What I wished to draw attention to was the fact that a, private member of parliament has a greater right to the use of the franking privilege during the session than a minister of the Crown, if I correctly interpret the hon. gentleman's own regulations.

It seems to me that it is time that a protest was put in against the remarks made by my hon. friend from Carle-ten, New Brunswick (Mr. Carvell). Eighty or ninety of us are new members, and I think it is fair to assume that the majority of us have come here with an earnest desire to do the best we can for this country, very often regardless of political affiliations. I am aware that hon. gentlemen opposite, and those on this side, are working along different lines, and unfortunately on many occasions there is too much party recrimination and bitterness. Now, the present discussion involves a principle, and I want to express my satisfaction with the way in which the Postmaster General has dealt with this question. He has recognized that there is a principle at stake, and has shown a manly and honest desire to rectify the abuse referred to. But when these matters are under discussion, and an hon. member opposite gets up and introduces totally irre-

levant matter, for the purpose of flinging a cheap jibe at the opposite party, I think it is time for any member who has a sincere desire for the progress of this country along right lines to enter a protest against the irrelevancy and the levity of his remarks.

We have gained a great deal when we have got from the minister a promise to try to rectify this evil. This frank is in plain blue pencil, and anybody might have made it, whether he had any authority or not. I was told at the post office that these were the initials of the hon. Minister of Agriculture, and I wish to ask that hon. gentleman whether he gave anybody authority to frank literature of this kind with his frank in blue pencil on the envelopes, or whether he knew it was done?
I did not give authority to anybody to frank with a blue pencil in any way or shape, and did not know it was done.

The question that has been discussed this afternoon is a little more important than probably the Solicitor General, from the way in which he met it, may think it to be. I consider it to be a very important question, because, as my hon. friend from British Columbia has said, there is a principle underlying it, and the Postmaster General has in that respect come face to face with it in a manly way and has acknowledged that there was an evasion of the Act, and has given the assurance to this House that, whether it was done by a colleague or by an outsider, he proposed to take what measures are necessary in order to prevent it occurring again. He went a little further: he proposed to investigate the matter and find out if he could what had been done, and what punishment or remedy could be enforced. If it was done with the authority of the Postmaster General or that of any of the ministers of the Crown, and if it was done with the authority of any of the ministers of the Crown after the session was over, they themselves would be responsible for the pecuniary damage and for any violation of the principle of the Act, if that were proved to have happened. But the fact is, and it is plain enough, that somebody has been robbing the public treasury. That is exactly what it means. Tf a man had gone into a country post office in the dead of night and abstracted from the till of the postmaster money belonging to the postal revenues, would he be a thief, or would he come before this House and say, I did it, I glory in it, and I am not going to make any apology for' it? It is plain what it means; and if $20 or $2,000 has been kept in the pocket of the man who by the law Ought to pay it into the Consolidated Fund of Canada for the service Canada did in carrying his mail matter, is it any less robbery of the public treasury? I do not think my hon. friend the Postmaster
General will deny that it is exactly the one and the same thing as the other. In the one ease your man comes and takes the money out in stealth by night; in the other case he robs the treasury just as effectively, because he either uses a power which he has no right to use or surreptitiously gets his carrying done without paying anything therefor. Now, we have three cases. We have the case of a private post card. No private post card can go through the postal service of this country without- a one cent stamp upon it.
Hear, hear.

This private post card is only one; but as long as there is the one which contravenes the law it is serious. When the hon. Postmaster General comes to investigate it, if he does, he might find out whether it slipped in between two others or not. Somebody must have posted it, and, prima facie, the man who posted it intended to defraud the revenue. No court or judge before whom the matter was tried would say that is probably how it happened. It is not the business of the judge and it is not the business of the Postmaster General, to suggest how it may have slipped in. There is the incriminating charge, and it is his business to suppose that his revenues have been defrauded, and to go as far as he can in tracing the fraud. That post card apparently was not posted at a, post office, but was put into a postal car on the railway between St. John or Campbellton and Halifax and sent to a gentleman at that time in the city of Halifax. There is one case; in how many cases was the same thing done? In the other case, what happened? The Solicitor General, if I understood him aright, took the ground that the matter that went out was good.
Will the Postmaster General examine that for a moment? If a man has defrauded the mails by putting a letter inside a news paper and so avoiding letter postage, is it any answer for him, when he is brought to bcok, to say :	1 But there were fine sentiments in that letter? Such an excuse would not be taken. Evidently, then, it is no excuse for the Solicitor General to say that the matter he sent out without paying the country's postage, as I believe he should have paid under the law, was good matter. This is not the kind of excuse that increases- very much our respect for the Justice Department of this country. Here is a man to whom we pay some thousands of dollars a year and his travelling expenses; he represents justice in this country ; ' before this House and this country he takes a position which I doubt if- any otner representative of a justice department has ever taken

that if the stuff is: good stuff it is no harm to send it through the mails without paying the proper legal postage. Here is a case in which the frank

is plain; the Postmaster General himself cannot cavil on that ground. If there is anything in the law on this subject, it is intended to preclude members of parliament or ministers from franking extraneous matter through the mails when the House is not in session. Extraneous matter, I say. I would not carry the prohibition too far. If a minister during recess wishes to write a letter to the firm of which he was a member, or to pay a bill, I would not object to his franking the letter. That is a point that no one would raise in this House. Every minister does it, I dare say, and no one would cavil at it. But has the minister a right to take my correspondence and save postage for me by franking it through the mails? He has not. Where, then, is the defence of the Solicitor General? What was this matter that was being sent out? Was it anything connected with the business of the Department of Justice? No. Was it anything connected with Mr. Ayles-worth's personal business? No. Was it anything connected with Mr. Jacques Bureau's personal business? No. Carry the case a little further. Mr. Aylesworth might have been writing to his constituents asking them to vote for him and to fight against Armstrong or whoever was going to be nominated ' against him. He might frank that letter; I would not find fault with that. But here is an organization that is conducting political warfare against nearly half the people, and it is so high-toned and so high-minded that it employs its Solicitor General to beat one of the departments that the government is trustee for, the Department of the Post Office, out of the petty postage on its letters. This weekly letter is an engine of the Liberal party; it is a part of its propagandist machinery, and is a matter entirely outside the personal business of Mr. Aylesworth or Mr. Bureau. It is posted every week of the year, in session or out of session, and is franked by the Justice Department. Does any one deny it? The solicitor General says that he has no apology for it. He might just as well frank the merchandise of the C. Ross Company on Sparks street. The great Liberal party ought to be more able than a private company to pay such expenses, and ought to be quite as manly to bear it. Will the Postmaster General inquire what the Liberal committee in the city of Ottawa were doing all last winter and up to the very day of election? If he does he will learn that tons and tons, millions and millions of copies of brochures and pamphlets were sent away from Ottawa under frank and scattered over every constituency in this country. I have here a statement by the secretary of that organization in the city of Ottawa stating exactly what was being sent out-so many copies of this or of that, to go into the several constituencies before election day.

Did the Liberal party pay any of that postage after the House was prorogued ? That is worth inquiring into. If this postage was not paid a wrong was done, somebody has robbed the treasury, and somebody should be punished for it. But there is worse than this, and I ask the Postmaster General (Mr. Lemieux) to pay attention. All this would be bad enough, but there is still more in it. Here is a Liberal-Conservative running in the county of Argenteuil. He gets up his own literature and pays for it. While he is a member of parliament he has a right to frank anything he likes into his county by way of propaganda-that is a matter between him and his constituency. But one day after the close of the session he has no such right. A Mr. McGibbon opposes him in his county-whether he was a candidate before the House closed or not T do not know. It would be bad enough for members of parliament or cabinet ministers to frank literature through the mails after session, but it appears that, again and again, those who never were members of parliament, who were not even nominated for parliament until after the House closed, sent their literature under frank, or had it sent in some way first to Ottawa and from Ottawa throughout the constituency. His Majesty's post office paid the bill; the public revenue loses that much. The frank of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) was used to defraud the revenue of a large amount. Here are two things, one of which is unfair and the other absolutely dishonest. It is unfair that the Liberal-Conservative candidate should have to bear his own expense, while the Liberal candidate, by reason of his party being in power, should be able to send his literature without expense, taking the money from the taxes of the Liberal-Conservatives as well as from those of the Liberals of this country. The Minister of Agriculture has not denied that he franked literature after the House was closed; he said it was possible that it might be his frank. I would be loath to believe that any one would have the gall to put the initials ' S.A.F.,M.A.' on envelopes and send them through the post office. I should be inclined to think, under the admission of the Minister of Agriculture, that he himself had so franked this literature, or had authorized it to be done. He will not deny that it may be his own; I cannot deny that it may be a forgery of his name. If Sir Richard Cartwright or Mr. Fielding makes a speech in parliament I have no objection to their sending them out by the thousands under frank. But I do not believe that they have the right to take up the campaign of Mr. McGibbon in his constituency and frank his literature. This matter cannot rest here. If it were treated by every one as it has been by the Postmaster General

we could leave it to him, but the Department of Justice has said that what they did was absolutely right and that they had no apology; they flaunted defiance in the face of this House. The matter must be tried out and we must know whether the government is going to put its imprimatur on a doctrine like that. I do not believe the government will. I give them credit for long consciences sometimes, but I do not think they will father that doctrine. I am sorry the Justice Department put itself in a position like that before this House and before the intelligent fourth estate 1 see before me, especially on this side of Mr. Speaker's chair, and before the country at large.

My hon. friends have referred to what appears to be my frank on certain literature that was sent out during the political campaign. I may be wrong in my interpretation of a minister's privilege in franking outside of the session, but I have always supposed that he has the same privilege as members of parliament have during the session of parliament.
Right.

Members of parliament during session were able to frank anything whatever it might be which they wished to send out connected with their public position as members of parliament. I believed that as a minister I had a right to frank anything I sent out relating to my public position as a minister. I do not know whether that was my frank or not; I certainly never gave authority to put a pencil frank in that way on any envelope. I do not know what the contents were. I do not think I should send out literature sent to me or my department by any one else under my frank. I think that would be improper, but I have always felt that I had a perfect right to frank during the recess such matters as members have been franking during the session. I have been acting upon that principle. If my interpretation of my privilege has been wrong, I am prepared to bow to the proper and legal interpretation and to forego such privilege in the future. I have acted upon that principle for many years, and I know that my predecessors in this and every other government have done the same thing. I know that members have franked tons of literature in each of the last three sessions. I am willing to stand by what I have done in the past, as I know that I have simply been following the practice of all other ministers.

I rise to endorse in a very few words what I consider was a noble appeal to this House, and to the new members on the part of the hon. member for Yale-Cariboo (Mr. Burrell.). I am certain he will get the ear of a large portion of this
country when he asks the members of this House to cease from mutual recrimination, and devote themselves to more imnortant work by example and by precept, of raising the public life of the country, and attending to the legislative and administrative business they were sent here to do. I thought when the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) rose to his feet and referred to the member for Yale-Cariboo (Mr. Burrell), that the hon. member for Yale-Cariboo had sown his seed upon ground where we might not have expected it to bring forth very good fruit, but where it had brought forth very good fruit, for the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) endorsed, as I understood in his opening words, the proposition laid down by the hon. member for Yale-Cariboo (Mr. Burrell). He said quite truly that there is a principle at stake in this thing, and the minister faced the principle nobly, boldly, and honestly, and promised that he would do his best to see that no abuse of this kind occurred. I take it that the response of the minister t-o the appeal which had been made to the whole House by the hon. member for Yale-Cariboo (Mr. Burrell) was perfect. But after this commencement what do we find the hon. member for North Toronto doing? I could not describe his speech better than by saying it was the most magnificent example of what had been described by the member for Yale-Cariboo in the term mutual recrimination How much further forward are we going to get by talking of one another as robbers and thieves? If that is not the language of recrimination, I do not know the meaning of the word. He appealed, as I understood him, to the great Liberal government as he described it, to show some high-mindedness. Wherever the Liberal government goes for its lessons in high-mindedness, the last place I should go is to the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster).
Oh, oh.
For the matter of that I do not think that if I did go I should be followed by many of his friends on that side of the House.
Oh, oh.

I am thoroughly in agreement with the logic of what has fallen from the lips of the Minister of Agriculture. I think the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) was not only wrong in taste in not following the very good advice given him, but that he was hopelessly weak in his logic. If members are to be allowed to break the law during the session, he may rely upon it that ministers will break the law during the recess. The whole weakness in the case of the opposition in this matter is to be found in a remark of the hon. member for Grey (Mr. Middlebro).

16IP
He said that he would restrict the franking privilege to members, or would even allow them to go a little over the mark. Well, we all go over the mark. Will the hon. member for North Toronto rise and say that he has never franked a letter for some one which, strictly interpreting, the law, he had no right to do? I notice that he loes not rise. If I wanted to imitate his picturesque and forcible style of oratory, I should point my linger at him and say that he was a robber and a. thief; but I abstain. Now, I would like to give the Postmaster General every encouragement to go along the line he has promised to pursue. After all, I wonder that hon. members on the opposition side of the House do not see that in all these discussions about political purity what they are really doing is aspersing their own country-that is what it amounts to in the end, they are aspersing their own country. They are attacking the morality of the people and of the nation to which we belong, because the practice of this government has just been endorsed by a majority of the people of this country. I do not think that the most Pharisaical man opposite would rise in his place and say that all the political morality of Canada is on the opposition side of the House of Commons. I do not believe that even the hon. member for North Toronto would be equal to that bold statement. They are attacking the people of this country, they are attacking the political morality of this country. The way to cure the evil is for ministers to face criticism such as this, boldly and honestly; it is for the House of Commons, to respond honestly, as individuals and as a corporate body, to such appeals as the member for Yale-Cari-boo (Mr. Burrell) has made to-day. I have responded to these appeals because I have fought two elections in this country; one of them I lost, and one of them I won. So far as I was personally concerned they were pure elections; I was not in a position to buy votes even if I could, and I would not buy them if I was able to do so. Let the electors be good enough not to be bought; let the candidates be good enough not to buy them, and you will soon see an improvement in the political morality of the country. With regard to the logic of this thing. I think my hon. friend is hopelessly wrong. If we are to have improvement in this matter, the franking right must be restricted to the utmost possible extent. You cannot break a law in little pieces. That would be the last word I would like to utter on this occasion.

I must say I like the
way in which the Minister of Agriculture spoke about this matter, and also the Postmaster General ; but I cannot understand how he could interpret the regulations Mr. M. CLARK.
in the way he says he did. Section 114, which refers to this subject, seems to me to be quite plain. Referring to mail that is sent out from Ottawa, it says:
All letters and other mailable matter posted from the public departments at Ottawa and franked as being of an official character.
That is all it says. When it refers to mail matter coming into Ottawa it says:
-all correspondence addressed to the ministers in charge of the said departments or to their private secretaries or to the deputy heads or secretaries
comes free. But in reference to mail matter going out, )the language is distinct, that the frank only covers matter of an official character. Now I cannot see by what stretch of imagination the Minister of Agriculture can claim that this campaign literature sent out all over the country, was a document of an official character. I do not suppose he will suggest that, so I cannot understand by what method of reasoning he reaches his conclusion. As I understand the regulations, during the session of the House we are all supposed to be on an equality. We are two parties in this country. Last session when we were sending out literature, we received every civility and service from the post office authorities here, everything was done to give us fair play, to gentlemen on this side equally with those opposite. Now during the session we are all on an equality, we all have a right to frank literature to our respective counties, or to any other county. But as I read this section 114, the moment a session of parliament is over, ministers of the Crown have no longer this right which belongs to members during the session; they then come back to their official right, which is limited strictly to 'the official business of this country. Now how can the Minister of Agriculture argue that that right extends to them during the recess ? I submit it would be exceedingly unfair during an election. We are all supposed to be on an equality. Opposition members have to pay postage on their literature during recess, and why should not their opponents pay postage also? I do not knqw how this was done whether the literature was sent in by the government candidates to Ottawa and franked out from here, or whether the Liberal party had an office here in Ottawa with a, staff of clerks engaged in writing those mystic letters on these envelopes.. But it was not fair play to the Conservative side. I would like to know how the Minister of Agriculture can imagine that section 114 of this Postal Guide gives him any authority to frank letters during recess, to other counties than his own?

I confess I have never carefully read the law. I knew what the practice had been from time immemorial,

and I followed it, supposing that my predecessors during their administration had followed the law.

The whole subject was discussed at great length in this Home about ten years ago, and the distinction which has been pointed out by the hon. member for Argenteuil (Mr. Perley) was clearly and forcibly pointed out at that time.
