During a session a member of parliament, as I recollect the regulation-I have not got it under my hand-is at liberty to send out literature, any documents, whether of a public or private nature, under his frank. I suppose the reason for that is obvious; it would be impossible in the post office to make any distinction between documents of a public character sent out by a member and those of a private character. At all events there is the language of the regulation, and you cannot put any restriction upon it so long as it remains as it is. But when you come to the power of a minister of the Crown outside of a session of parliament, the language is very different; a minister's power to use his frank is restricted, as I have always understood it, to documents of an official character. Therefore, there is no confusion or lack of logic, as has been suggested, in the position taken on this side of the House. I do not think my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture was complying with the law in doing what he has acknowledged that he did on this occasion. The regulation with respect to a member of parliament, is in these words:
Letters and other mailable matter addressed to or by any member of the Senate or of the House of Commons while at Ottawa, during any session of parliament, or to any such member at Ottawa, during the ten days next before the meeting of parliament, may pass free of postage.
Now with regard to ministers of the Crown, the case is entirely different.
All letters and other mailable matter posted from the public departments at Ottawa and franked as being of an * official character-
Shall pass through the post office free. Campaign literature can not properly or legally be franked as being of an official character; the Minister of Agriculture will recognize that at once. Thus, there is this very important difference, a difference which ought to be recognized and adhered to by a minister of the Crown so long as the regulations are in the form in which we find them at the present time.

I have followed very closely this debate and I reiterate the statement that some regulations should be framed so as to draw the line between use and abuse. In this matter, we have trusted to the personal honour and sense of propriety of members of the
House. I will not go so far as to say, as did my hon. friend from North Toronto, that, because there was some literature flanked during the recent campaign, some of the heads of these departments should be accused of theft and robbery. I say that might have been an abuse, but I would not go so far as to say that it was a crime. At all events, the regulations must be made clearer and I intend to frame them in such a way as will, in the future, not lead to the imputation of motives to either side of this House. Before the end of the sesion I may have occasion to discuss this question again and I hope everybody will find that justice will be done to both parties.

I do not want the idea to go abroad, as the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) has sought to convey it, that I have been engaged in robbing the country ever since I have been Solicitor General. The hon. gentleman has had his innings now and he is always happy to give me a crack when the opportunity offers, and I suppose he now feels satisfied. When he got up he had in his mind one of two things, either that he wanted to heap some abuse upon myself, or else he felt that he was standing by a principle and desired to have an evil corrected. As my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) has said, the hon. gentleman has himself franked a letter for another, but it does not follow that he is a public thief, and ought to be branded as such in the country. If I franked this weekly letter I did not do it to save money. I am not so close or stingy. I did it because it had been done before, as I well knew, because I have in my possession papers and other documents that were franked by ministers of the Crown under the old regime ad: dressed to myself and my father. It may be that under a strict interpretation of the regulations I was wrong, but when I said that I had no apology to make I said so with a full appreciation of my words. 1 never thought the hon. member for North Toronto was getting so careful of the public treasury and was becoming so close that all of a sudden he would make a crime of it. This is a usage which has prevailed for years which is now stronger, not only than the regulations but than the law itself. It has been done for many years, and if so where are you going to draw the line? I made the statement that I thought I was not violating the law and I repeat that I never thought I was violating the law, because I never thought that for years and years and years such a violation could take place without a remedy being provided. I franked this letter because it was in accordance with the usage, and now my hon. friend wants to convey to the country the idea that I have set up as my justification the claim that it was good matter. I never
1G33

made any such statement. My hon. friend with all his volubility of language and his wonderful imagination, can take out of my words, maybe misplaced, what I never meant, in odder to put an improper interpretation upon them and to impute a wrong purpose. I made this statement because the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. J. D. Taylor) said that this letter was something that was indecent, and should not go through the mails.
Mr. Chairman, 1 rise to a point of order. I object to be misrepresented by the Solicitor General. I never made any such statement.
How did you qualify that letter?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman says that he did not make that statement you must not insist.
It may be that I am mistaken. I do not want to misrepresent the hon. gentleman, but he did qualify it. Have I not the right to ask him how he qualified it?
Scurrilous.

Thank you. He called it ' scurrilous ' matter; that is no better. I do not want it to be said that I stood here and bragged that I had done it. I said that I had no apology to make for what I have done, and I repeat it. My hon. friend does not expect me to run across the floor, cross my hands, get down on my knees before him and say: Oh thou, the only virtuous man on earth, forgive me! I will not do it. I did only what has been done for years and a thing which would not justify anybody in holding it up to the country as a threat against the welfare of Canada. If we have robbed the country, notwithstanding all our thieveries the Postmaster General is able to come here to-day and make the statement that the Post Office Department, instead of having a deficit, as it had in years past, finishes the year with a surplus, and I will leave it to the people to judge if the exercise of the franking privilege has been the cause of a less efficient service, or of deficits. I do not want to incriminate the hon. member for North Toronto, but I know that he used to carry stamps around with him all the time to post letters to his family when he .was a minister of the Crown. [DOT] I do not want the hon. member for North Toronto to make an unjust attack upon the Minister of Justice, for whom I know he has a special love, because I said that I had no apology to make for what I had done. I speak for myself and myself alone.

It is a playful habit for some of my good friends on the other side of the House, if they are new members, to immediately lead an attack upon the mem-Mr. BUREAU.
ber for North Toronto. He seems to be a form of ladder on which to climb towards a sudden notoriety if nothing more in the House. I do not know how to explain it. There may be some natural explanation; I am not quite sure. I suppose a fly would rather make its onset on the horns of the ox than be flittering around the dust heap or something of that kind. There may be a principle in human nature that thinks that nobility comes out of that kind of thing. It is also the playful habit of some hon. gentlemen to impute to me what I did not say. The Postmaster General came very close to doing that. I was drawing a lesson, I drew it properly, I drew it in very plain, definite language so that any man could understand what I said, and I declared that there was no shadow of difference between the man who went into a post office at the dead of night and by stealth and secrecy burglarized the post office, and thus robs the treasury, and a man who surreptitiously and wrongfully put mail matter into the service and had it carried at the instance of the country thereby making the country pay the bill; it was jobbing the revenues just the same. When you discuss a principle and try to make two things equal, you are not under any conscious knowledge, until you are taken up a moment. afterwards, that you called the Solicitor General a thief, that you called the Postmaster General a robber and that you called the Minister of Agriculture a burglar or anything of that kind. Some class of minds may reason that way; I am not responsible for every class of mind that there is in this country, and I suppose I have to be under a disability on that account. Now, my hon. friend grew rather dramatic-it is allowable to him-and he figuratively crossed the House, dropped on his-I am afraid not very hardened-knees, and apostrophized the member for North Toronto as the only virtuous man. That is a lovely little failing the members on the other side of the House have. They think it is a manly way of making a statement which they do not care to make on their own responsibility. My good and recently acquired friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) started out nob' y and had he only stopped where he started he would be farther ahead than he was at the end, because he started with the enunciation of the principle that we were not to have recrimination in this House and he did not go far before he wondered whether he would come to the member for North Toronto as_ an example of high mindedness.
For lessons in high mindedness; quote accurately.

Yes, for lessons in high mindedness. Now, what did my hon. friend mean by that? Did he mean to start out on the principle of brotherly amity that was enunciated by my hon. friend from Yale-

Cariboo (Mr. Burrell)? He may have thought he was on that skating rink but it seemed to me he was floundering on ice far away. He went on to make two or three other allusions; what did they mean? Had they anything to do with this argument? Starting from his hypothesis he should not have used them because they introduced the principle of scrap between the parties, and that was a thing his soul abhorred. Now my hon. friend, was I not right in saying that had you stopped where you started your ground would have been, more logical than it was at the end?
It would have been better for you.

Well, I suppose that remark is on the principle that the fly that jabs at the bull's horn thinks he is doing a tremendous piece of battle, and if it pleases the fly and does not hurt the bull, I suppose there is no great harm in it; it is just a question for the onlooker and the outsider who is not prejudiced either way to form a judgment upon. Now, the whole thing is simply this: The member for Three Eivers, although he may not realize it- sometimes we think he has not quite realized it-is a little more than simply a member of the House; he is the Solicitor General of Canada. He is a part of the Justice Department of this country, and he can hardly make a statement such as he has made this afternoon and disassociate himself from his department and from his position. We look to the Department of Justice-whether it is the minister or whether it is the Solicitor General, we look to him as an exponent of the law, and I allowed myself in an unguarded moment to make a query as to whether one who seemed to have come so far short of a proper definition of this law would shed lustre and brilliance upon the department to which, for some reason or other unknown to most of us, he has been for some years allied.
At six o'clock the House took recess.

House resumed at eight o'clock.

House in committee on Bill (No. 44) to incorporate the Canadian, Liverpool and Western Eailway Company.-Mr. Girard.
On section 2,
The works of the company are declared to be for the general advantage of Canada.

subsubtopic: CANADIAN, LIVEEPOOL AND WESTEEN EAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: This raises a question which has been suggested in this House before and which was discussed at some length in the Eailway Committee-the propriety of putting such a clause as this into Acts of parliament without reference to the truth of the statement thus made. I raised the question in committee. I do not question, nor has anybody ever questioned, so far as I know, the constitutional power of this House to declare a work to be for the general advantage of Canada. Nor does anybody question the fact that, when parliament makes this declaration concerning any given work, then, under the clause of the British North America Act, the work becomes legally one for the general advantage of Canada. I do not wish to occupy the attention of the House at length, but I desire to protest formally and strongly against the idea apparently entertained by members of this House that there is no question to be considered in reference to inserting such a provision in a Bill as to whether the statement thus made is true or false. Some hon. members seem to think that because parliament has the power to declare a work to be for the general advantage of Canada, that settles the question, and that if we exercise our powers that makes it all right. What I contend is that the constitution intended and requires that before the House expresses such an opinion by Act of Parliament, it should satisfy itself of the truth of the statement; it should be convinced that the work is really one for the advantage of Canada as a whole. I am convinced, from what passed in the committee the other day, that the question whether this work is or is not one for the general advantage of Canada was not considered. This subject has been before the House again and again, and with all respect to the House, I say that the matter has been dealt with without regard to the truth or falsity of the statement made, that this declaration that a work is for the general advantage of Canada has been put into Acts of Parliament when, in my opinion, it was actually false, and without hon. members considering for one moment whether the statement was true or the very opposite of true. We have spent hours and hours in discussing such questions and without much result. But I do not propose to let a Bill of this kind pass thi^ House without entering my protest against the practise that I have just mentioned. The constitution intended that the provinces should control certain works within their confines, but it gave to this parliament the power and right, when it found a ease to warrant it, to declare a work, even though within provincial limits, to be a work for the general advantage of Canada, and therefore one to be controlled by this parliament. I protest against such a statement being put into a Bill of this kind without due consideration, and against any hon. member voting in favour of inserting such a statement in a Bill unless he is convinced that the statement is true.

subsubtopic: CANADIAN, LIVEEPOOL AND WESTEEN EAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I am not directly or indirectly interested in this Bill, except as a member of this House and a member of the Railway Committee. Nor do I take exception to the argument of my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker); in fact, I quite concur with him on the question of principle. I believe that, unless there is within the scope of the corporation^ objects that are interprovincial or international in their character, we should not attempt to incorporate such a body or give it any powers. This Bill was very fully considered by the committee. I know nothing with respect to the objects of the company or the gentlemen who seek to be incorporated except what appears in the Bill. In the Bill certain objects are set forth, and it is clear that it is the intention of the incorporators to do a transcontinental and export business, to place themselves in a position to make connection with through railways and steamships and to have steamships of their own. My hon. friend (Mr. Barker) need only refer to clause A of section 8. Or, if that does not satisfy him, let him refer to section 13, wherein it is stated that these gentlemen who seek incorporation desire to form a company that can enter into agreement with transcontinental railway companies, the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Grand Trunk, the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian Northern of Quebec, showing clearly that the object of this railway is to do an interprovincial, transcontinental and even international traffic. There is also clause A of section 10 which covers the right to engage in a navigation enterprise in connection with their railway, clearly having in view an export business. Now, I quite appreciate this fact -that, unless upon the facts we can declare that the work is for the general advantage of Canada we should not listen to the prayer of the petition. But if they desire to have power to do business that is beyond the limits of one province and so come within the jurisdiction of this parliament, it seems to me that in such a case it is for us to give them their powers, because they cannot get them elsewhere. The .moment we are not able to declare that the works of a company are for the general advantage of Canada, we are without jurisdiction and have no power even to enact such legislation; it is ultra vires of this parliament. A provincial legislature could incorporate these gentlemen, but could not grant them the powers asked for under sections 13, 10 and 8 of this Bill.

subsubtopic: CANADIAN, LIVEEPOOL AND WESTEEN EAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Is there any doubt that a provincial legislature can authorize its own creation to make any. ..contract with another company that has powers partly from the legislature creating that company?

subsubtopic: CANADIAN, LIVEEPOOL AND WESTEEN EAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: That would have to be ratified by this parliament.

subsubtopic: CANADIAN, LIVEEPOOL AND WESTEEN EAILWAY COMPANY.
CANADIAN, LIVEEPOOL AND WESTEEN EAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Not at all.

subsubtopic: CANADIAN, LIVEEPOOL AND WESTEEN EAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: However, that is entirely begging the question; they could not get the powers asked in section 13. These jealousies that are stirred up as between the provincial and Dominion government are, I think, not in the best interests of either the province or the Dominion. Wherever a transportation company can come within the scope of the Dominion parliament, I think it is in the interests of transportation in this country that they should come here and that we should incorporate them. It is all important in the interests of transportation that the Railway Commission should have jurisdiction over the companies, certainly over railway companies seeking to make traffic agreements with other railroad corporations in other provinces, so that the railways may be subject to the orders of the commission. In the case of a purely local or provincial corporation the company should not come within the scope of the Dominion Railway Commission. I do not take issue with my hon. friend in his theory. All that he has said is very true, but it is not applicable to the circumstances of this Bill. That is why I supported the Bill in the committee. I would hesitate to support the granting of a Dominion charter to any railway, purely provincial in character. I am just as zealous in that regard as is my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker). I speak for myself as one member of the committee, and only for myself.

subsubtopic: CANADIAN, LIVEEPOOL AND WESTEEN EAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: The hon. member (Mr. Emmerson) argues strongly that a provincial railway could not take advantage of the provision of clause 13, could not enter into agreements in regard to the handling of freight, &c. The Ontario and Northern Railway, which is entirely provincial, has entered into agreements with Dominion railways, and no trouble has resulted. This is done with many railways.

subsubtopic: CANADIAN, LIVEEPOOL AND WESTEEN EAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Would the Railway Commission have power to exercise any jurisdiction over that provincial entity?

subsubtopic: CANADIAN, LIVEEPOOL AND WESTEEN EAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
There are two Railway Commissions, the provincial and the Dominion, and the provincial commission has jurisdiction over provincial railways just as the Dominion has over Dominion railways. This company professes to desire to carry on transportation by navigation, but we find it is too frequently the ease that companies ask for rights of this kind, or the right to build storehouses or elevators, or to navigate inland wateTs, which in all probability they will never do, but abandon these rights of their charters and depend on the other features of their charters. We had a Power Bill before the House a few days ago. It originally applied to three rivers, the Rainy river, which

was international, the Nipigon which was navigable, and the Pigeon, which was neither navigable nor international. The Pigeon river was dropped from the Bill this year. I believe that the other two streams were taken in in order to get away from the control and jurisdiction of the provinces, on the grounds that one was a navigable river and the other an international stream. When a work is to be declared for the general advantage of Canada the promoter should be made to show that it is in reality for the general advantage. That phase in a Bill should not be a mere allegation Without any tangible foundation. This railway is all in the province of Quebec and the Quebec legislature could incorporate the company and give them power to do anything they desire to do. We had a representative of the provincial government come before our committee and protesting in the strongest way that it was an invasion of provincial rights, and would likely lead to trouble if it was continued. Surely we ought to have some respect for representatives of provincial governments when they come before us and tell us that we are invading their rights. We should have the strongest ground for doing so, otherwise we will be doing what the hon. gentleman says we ought to avoid, that is, creating difficulties between the provinces and the federal government. That is what we are doing here, and when we have representatives from the province protesting against it, saying that they have a right to give all the powers requisite to enable this corporation to carry out the purposes of its undertakings within a province, and in face of that are we going to usurp their authority by stating in this parliament that it is a work for the general advantage of Canada, and take it under our own control, and deprive the provinces of the control they are entitled to exercise? I think we should go very slowly on this question. As my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) has said this question has been argued over and over again, and we have not been able to make our opinions prevail. The question is becoming more intense every year. The province of Ontario comes down here from time to time; there are several Bills on the paper of a similar character in which that province is interested. Last year they sent down their representatives, and I am told will do the same this year, to remonstrate against the invasion of provincial rights. The province of Quebec is doing its best to avoid the difficulty, the province of Ontario is putting forth all its influence to avoid it, and if, in face of these facts, we do over and over again invade provincial rights, we must in the end provoke a contest that will lead to no good results. I think we would be well advised if we took an early opportunity of ascertaining what the respective rights of the provinces and the Dominion are, so that we may keep within our rights, and not always be infringing upon the rights of the provinces. The more we do so the greater will be the trouble, and the more difficult will be a settlement in the future when this question comes to a climax, as it undoubtedly will some time.

subsubtopic: CANADIAN, LIVEEPOOL AND WESTEEN EAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
I agree somewhat with the hon. member for East Grey (Mr Sproule) when he claims that there should be a principle laid down to guide us in matters of this kind. We have had this question before the Railway Committee many times during the last three or four years, in fact there is hardly a Bill coming before the Railway Committee asking that a work be declared for the general advantage of Canada, on which we have not heard the question of provincial rights discussed. I do not intend to discuss the reasons why I should vote for this Bill, because I am willing to adopt the reasons advanced by my hon. friend from Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson). I think he has stated sufficient reasons to justify us in voting for the Bill. But I want to go further than that. There seems to be a doctrine advanced by many hon, gentlemen, especially those from Ontario, that we have no right to grant legislation or to create an entity if it be wholly within any province of Canada. Now I want to refer the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) and also the member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker)-and they are both reasonable men, the hon. member for Hamilton is no doubt a good lawyer-I want them to be fair, and tell this House whether, in their opinion, section 92 of the British North America Act did not contemplate just such legislation as is being proposed in this Bill, if it did not contemplate that this parliament should have the right to create a corporation for the purpose of doing business entirely within the province. Take clause (c) of subsection 10 of section 92, you will find that it especially exempts from the jurisdiction of provincial legislatures such works as, although wholly situated w'ithin the province, are, before or after their execution, declared by the parliament of Canada to be for the general advantage of Canada, or for the advantage of two or more provinces. Therefore the British parliament, when the British North America Act was being put through, specially contemplated that the federal parliament of Canada should have the right to create corporations for the purposes of carrying on works wholly within the province so long as that work was to the general advantage of Canada. But now the question arises on what principle should this narliament proceed in order to decide when any particular proposition is or is not for the general advantage of Canada? It seems to me that is an important thing for this parliament to consider, that is a thing we have been dis-

cussing in the Railway Committee ever since I have been a member of parliament and it is being discussed more and more every year. I believe with my hon. friend from East Grey that the time has arrived when a clear definition should be made, not of what are our rights, because we have all the rights possible, but when we should exercise our rights, and when we should refrain from exercising them. I think that is a fair proposition.
Now probablv I would go further than the hon. member for Hamilton, I would go so far as to say that a Bill, having for its purpose the incorporation of a railway company to connect with any 'other railwav company operated by steam, should h" incorporated by this parliament and not by the provincial legislature. I put forward that proposition for this reason:	To my
mind the greatest function which the Railway Commission ought to have in Canada is the regulation of rates and the preservation of life and property. Now I make the statement, I know my hon. friend from Hamilton will agree with me, that the Railway Commission has no power to regulate traffic rates over a railway created by a provincial legislature; therefore, in order to give the Railway Commission any control over the rates of a railroad we must have it created by the federal parliament and not by a provincial legislature. My hon. friend can see the difficulty he will be met with the very moment that a railway created by a local legislature attempts to do business with a railway, or make connection with a railway which is of a Dominion character. This petition asks for the right to build a railway from a point on the Transcontinental Railway to other places. It starts from a connection with a Dominion railroad, necessarily, when it is completed, it must come in contact with the Canadian Pacific Railway, with the Canadian Northern of Quebec, and probably with the old Grand Trunk Railway. Now if a man living on the line of this railway wishes to ship goods to any other portion of Canada he has got to get a rate from this road in conjunction with the other roads; or if he wants to bring goods from any portion of Canada into any other portion of Canada, he must get a through rate from the point of shipment to the point of distribution, and that means a rate over the Dominion road as well as over the local road. My hon. friend will agree with me that the Railway Commission has no power to control those rates, if this railroad is incorporated by the province of Quebec.

speechtext:
(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, as I am responsible for the bringing up of this question before the railway committee yesterday, I may be allowed to say a word.
Whatever may have been the mode of procedure followed heretofore, and altogether the words 'work for the general advantage of Canada ' may have been in most cases inserted in Bills of a similar nature, I do not think that the constitution of our country has; been modified in consequence. I, for one, consider that the whole matter turns on the question as to whether we havel the right and authority required for inserting that clause in such Bills.
In turn, I may be allowed to read the article of the constitution just quoted by the hon. gentleman for Carleton (Mr. Car-vell), though I am bound to give it a) different meaning:
Sec. 92, paragraph c., ' Such works as, although wholly situate within the province, are before or after execution declared by the parliament of Canada to be for the general advantage of Canada or for the advantage of two or more of the provinces.'
It will thus be seen that such works should before or after their execution be declared to be for the general advantage of Canada. In a charter like this statements of all kinds may be inserted. For instance, I may request authority to build a railway in the city of Ottawa, with power to extend the line into the United States; but my requesting such authority does not in itself, to my mind, suffice to endow the Dominion parliament with the enabling power required. It frequently occurs that people who ask for charters for such undertakings have no great assurance of being in a position to carry them on very far, and the idea seems to be that the inserting of such a clause will give this parliament jurisdiction That is not my belief. To my mind, some evidence of one's intents and means is required. Yesterday, before the committee, no attempt was made to show that this undertaking was for the advantage of Canada. That is where such evidence should have been adduced, as it is known that when such a Bill is referred back to the House, such proof is supposed to have been made. Inserting in the Bill this or that statement does not give parliament jurisdiction. In the present instance, no attempt even has been made to show that this undertaking was for the general interest of Canada.
All these clauses inserted in Bills, as for instance those in Section 13, which empower the company to enter into arrangements with the Grand Trunk, Canadian Pacific Railway and other railway companies, are no evidence at all, and often
have for their sole object to enable the promoters to sell out to other companies. These gentlemen might just as well have asked for a grant of all the franchises mentioned in the revised statutes, so as to be in a position to sell them at some time or other. Very often things are managed just in that fashion.
If such a principle were to be accepted, provincial rights would be utterly destroyed, and there would be no sense in a local legislature granting charters, since the Dominion parliament would have control over everything I understand that when a railway has been created under a provincial charter, and it becomes necessary, on account of its extension, to declare it a work 'for the general advantage of Canada,' the Dominion parliament may so declare it; but I maintain that such a step may be taken only after the undertaking has been carried out. On the other hand, if it should be found desirable to make such a declaration before going on with the undertaking, some evidence as to its truth should be required. This is precisely what was omitted before the committee yesterday.
I protest against the habit of inserting into all such Bills a general clause of this character, without any attempt at all at proving that such works are for the 'general advantage of Canada.'

speechtext:
In this connection, I have as much respect for provincial rights as any man in the House. I believe they should be respected but in the matter of railways I do not think there is room for any two opinions as to whether all railways in Canada having an interchange of commerce and traffic should be under the direction, control and influence of the Dominion Railway Commission. We have, in our neighbours to the south of us a striking illustration that we should not follow. There all the great railways endeavour, if possible, in their connecting links, to get a short road that is operated by a State charter, that is beyond the influence of the Interstate Commerce Law, because on these short branches, they are able to collect extortionate tolls on traffic that passes over them. In fact, -the great roads of the United States all have short lines of railway and they invariably, if at all possible, route traffic over these lines, explaining, in many cases where they have parallel or alternative lines, that they have no working arrangement with the lines that they directly control, but that they have working arrangements with the lines which they own and hold by trustees for their own good and welfare. For that reason the Interstate Commerce Commission has no jurisdiction and shippers are charged extortionate rates. Surely, if it is at all possible to prevent it, we should not create a condition of that kind in Canada. As has been said, those

railways which are strictly within the province should be chartered by the province and should be under the control of the province. If they limited their business entirely to the province, and did not come in conjunction with the general railways of the country the objection possibly would not be so great, but there is no railway, long or short, that proposes to do a business at all but has to have arrangements for the interchange of traffic with other railways and when they begin to do that, and they cannot exist without doing it, they should certainly come under 'the direction and control of the Dominion Railway Commission.
The Temiscaming and Northern Ontario railway has been held up as an illustration, but I know ffom my own experience and from correspondence with officials of, that road and of the Grand Trunk Railway that we are unable in many cases to compel them to quote rates because it does not come under the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission. It can, as I understand only be compelled to make traffic arrangements with the other railways by the good will of these other railways. I believe that the Temiscaming and Northern Ontario, good and all as it is in this province, ought by some means or other be brought under the Dominion Railway Commission. The province of Ontario has a provincial railway commission and they can control certain matters, but it is seldom that two commissions with different authority will agree, and so the best results cannot be obtained. Freight originating in the western provinces and shipped to the seaboard or on a through rate to the old country would lose not only the advantage of railway competition but of ocean competition as well, because under the arrangement which the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway have with the ocean liners, the through rates to the old country are' fairly steady and settled. This railway, with perhaps new terminals in Montreal and Quebec that will accommodate tramp steamers and all kinds of carriers which give lower rates for the heavier and coarser traffic, would be in a position to absorb all that difference and notwithstanding that the trunk lines would give as cheap rates from Vancouver and the west through to a junction near Montreal or Quebec, this little junction railway would be outside the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission and in that way they could extort a toll that would leave very little if any advantage for the shipper by reason of this alternate route. There does not seem any sound reason why any strip of railway should be permitted to do interchange of traffic business unless it is brought under the direction of the Dominion Railway Commission. While, in many matters it is perhaps right to stick Mr. SEA LET.
to the provincial rights idea to the letter it is not a consideration at all, to my way of thinking, in the matter of railways doing a general interchange transportation business.
