I take very strong objection to the position laid down by the Minister of Agriculture as to the right of a minister to frank mail matter outside of what appertains to the business of his own department during the recess of parliament. When I noticed the large circulation through the mails of this campaign literature in my county, I drew the attention of the people to the manner in which the revenue of the country was being defrauded in the interests of the government candidate in that country, and I naturally argued that the man who would do that sort of thing was not the man to send to parliament. I believe that was a fair and proper argument. The Minister of Agriculture has now argued that he considers that a min-' ister has the right during the recess to frank any mail matter that he sees fit, notwithstanding that it may have no reference whatever to the business of his own department. I raise my protest against the statement of the Minister of Agriculture because I feel that if I allowed it to go unchallenged, the argument I made during the campaign would be unfounded. I believe that the Postmaster General is quite in sympathy with my contention, that no minister of the Crown has the right to frank such campaign literature. On examining the frank on this envelope I believe it to be the frank of a minister of the Crown-I will not mention fris name-who occupies a seat in another house, and I fear it is but a repetition of what occurred years ago. Again I protest against this unfair and illegal use of the franking privilege by a minister. It would be monstrous if a minister of the Crown could, during

the parliamentary interim, frank everything and anything he thought fit, by the ton or the hundred tons, contrary to the regulations, which are explicit and clear that he has the right to frank only matter that has some connection with his department. I have said this in order to justify myself, and not to leave unchallenged the statement that was made this afternoon or to leave my people to suppose that I had raised a point during the election which was not tenable.

This afternoon I asked the hon. Postmaster General a question in regard to the salaries of letter carriers. I may remind him that his superintendent made certain recommendations to the Civil Service Commission in this matter, and in the Civil Service Act of last session I believe the salaries of the class to which letter carriers belong were placed at from $500, as a minimum, to $800, as a maximum. The recommendations of Mr. Ross, I think, put the salaries on a per diem basis instead of a yearly basis, and included some other recommendations, especially one relating to superannuation. I would like the minister to tell us whether he intends to adopt any of these recommendations of Mr. Ross, and if so, when?

I had not forgotten that question. My hon. friend, and indeed all the other members of the House, are very anxious that something should be done not only for the inside service, but also for the outside service. However, it is not a question of sympathy; it is a question of business. Whatever may be the sympathy of the incumbent of the Post Office Department, he has to submit to the wish of the government as a unit. Being myself a son of a poor civil servant, my sympathies, of course, go towards the outside civil servants. I am not at liberty, however, to place an amount in the estimates to give an increase to the letter carriers and the clerks in the pest offices. I am governed by the Post Office Act, which establishes different grades and fixes the salaries of the different classes. Since I have been acting as Postmaster General I have received delegation after delegation, and I can claim a little credit for having myself asked for the appointment of the recent Civil Service Commission. I have read the whole of the report, including the evidence given by each of the very able employees of the department, such as the deputy Postmaster General, the acting Deputy Postmaster General, and the chief superintendent, who are in daily contact with the employees. I have my own views on the subject, and although I cannot take the House into my confidence just now, as to what will be done in the near future, I may say that the acting deputy minister has prepared with myself a report which will be before council very shortly, on this very question of salaries 54
for the outside service in the Post Office Department. All I can say at present is that the matter is engaging the attention of the government.

The minister this afternoon made the statement that the moment a railway was built, advantage was taken of it to carry the mails by the trains. I do not think that has always been the case. I have just had letters from two small towns in my constituency, Odessa and Davin, which are situated on the Brandon and Regina branch of the Canadian Northern Railway, asking that they should have regular mail service carried by the trains. A train is run each way every day, and yet these places are receiving their mails only once a week, by means of the overland stage route. I imagine it likely that these would not be the only places along the line which are in the same position. If the Postmaster General will go into that question, and take advantage of the daily train service to provide a daily mail for the people, it will be very much in the interest of the country.

These two towns are on the main line of the railway, and I see no reason why they should be deprived of the railway mail service. If my hon. friend will make the usual application, the department will certainly look with favour on his request.
I heard that they had already applied to the department.
These things take time. There is a little red tape, but we try to avoid delay as far as possible. I see no reason why they should not have a daily mail.

I regret the conclusion the Postmaster General has come to with respect to the remuneration of the letter carriers, and I feel that he also regrets the stand that he is obliged to take. It seems to me that no work of the post office is more important than that of those who are delivering the mail, either a letter carrier or railway mail clerks. We ought to pay our officials in that capacity remuneration equivalent to that paid those similarly situated in other countries. For instance, in the United States men engaged in this work are very much better paid than in Canada. The work done by these men is onerous; it calls for men of education, strong men both in mind and body. In addition, the railway mail clerks take their lives in their hands when they engage in their work. The letter carriers perform an excellent service and receive small remuneration and enjoy few privileges. I had thought to raise this question when the Civil Service Bill was under consideration, but this seems a favourable opportunity. I would call the attention of the Postmaster General to the fact that the earning power



of his department is very large. Take, for instance, Toronto, which yields a large postal revenue, quite the largest of any city in Canada. It does seem to me that the men who perform there the work of letter carriers should receive something more than $1.25 or $1.50 a day. The statute, it is true, limits the minister's powers in this matter. But there is surely a way to amend Acts of this kind, and it is for the government to take the initiative in relieving the hardships of government employees wherever they exist. No one would oppose the appropriation of a reasonable sum to remunerate these men for services performed. I urge upon the minister very full consideration of this matter. The subject is one upon which the public feel deeply. Unfortunately, we see occasionally accounts of men in the post office service who betray their trust. In all such cases there is a public sentiment for the man who is receiving a mere pittance of $1.25 or $1.50 a day and is tempted to pilfer a letter. These men are trustees of money as well as performers of an important public service. I do hope that the minister's statement that this matter is under consideration is something substantial, that he means that the matter is to be dealt with in a way to give satisfaction to the public. After all, it is public service and the public pay for it. The Post Office yields a large revenue, and I do not think it is expected by the public that the Post Office is to be made a taxing department; we are satisfied if a good postal service is given and the department makes both ends meet. The public wants the best service they can get, and they want to pay fairly for efficiency. I am not one of those who believe that it is wise to ring a bell in the public street and call upon those who will undertake to work at low rates to enter the service. The men who do this work should be treated as the rest of the service are treated. They should not be regarded as being in the outside service; they are in the service of the country, in the service of the King, and they should be given a fair day's wage for a fair day's work. The minister will not hear any cavil on this side if he improves the condition of the men of whom I have been speaking, men whom the public believes to be entitled to more than they are receiving.

I desire to say a word especially upon behalf of the railway mail clerks. I agree with what my hon. friend from South Toronto (Mr. A. C. Macdonell) has said, that these men occupy a very hazardous position-I may say the most hazardous position in the public service. If any men in the public service deserve an increase, they are the railway mail clerks. By way of illustration, I may refer to an accident that happened a short time Mr. MACDONELL.
ago in my own constituency. The local train carrying the mail between Pembroke and Ottawa ran into a light locomotive. On that train were two railway mail clerks, and both these men were injured, not to any great extent, I understand, but one of them so seriously that he has been unable to resume work up to the present time. I should be very glad to see an increase given to these officials.
Is there a minimum salary for country postmasters?
Are there any cases in which they are paid a merely nominal sum -less than the minimum?
No.
How long has this minimum been in force?

In 1896,-speaking of the new era-the minimum salary of rural postmasters was $10. This applied to postmasters whose offices yielded almost no revenue. In 1897, or 1898, Sir Wm. Mu-lock increased that minimum to $25, and at the same time he increased the percentage given to the postmasters on postal notes and money orders. This was a good thing for the accounting offices. The small offices that do not sell postal notes or issue money orders are called non-accounting offices. Two years ago, I increased the minimum to $35 a year. I made another scale which I have not under my hand, of percentages for the sale of money orders and postal notes. I also made a larger allowance for rent, fuel, and light. On the whole the increase has been found satisfactory. The scale of increases is fully explained in this circular to postmasters:
Post Office Department, Canada,
Ottawa, September 17, 1907.
Postmasters are informed that the Postmaster General, after careful consideration of representations made by those postmasters whose salaries are based on the revenue of their offices, has decided on the following scale of remuneration.
Salary.
Fifty per cent on the first $1,000 of revenue, 30 per cent on all over $1,000 and up to $10,000, and 20 per cent on all over $10,000 of revenue, the minimum salary to be $35.
Allowance for Night Duty.
An allowance will be paid for night duty when a postmaster is required to he on duty after 9 p.m. or before 7 a.m. The minimum allowance will be $10, and the maximum $100, according to the time employed, and the work done.
Allowance for Forward Duty.
The rate of remuneration will be 12J per cent on the revenue of the offices for which direct or indirect forward duty is performed.

Allowance for Rent, Light and Fuel.
This allowance is to be increased by 35 per cent. Therefore, if a postmaster is now receiving $100 under this head, he will receive $125 under the new scale.
Compensation for the transaction of Money Order, Savings Bank, and Postal Note Business.
Money Order Business.
Four cents for each money order issued, and one cent for each order paid. Formerly postmasters were paid | per cent on the amount of all orders issued, and | per cent on the amount of foreign orders paid. This scale operated unfairly. For instance, while the work involved in the issue of a $100 order is no greater than in the issue of a $5 order, the commission the postmaster received from the $100 order was 25 cents, whilst for the $5 older only If cents. The system of paying so much a piece for the issue and payment of order is fairer in that the remuneration follows the work, and the rates above proposed will give the postmasters a somewhat better commission than they receive at present.
Savings Bank Business.
The rate of remuneration will remain as heretofore.
Postal Note Business.
One cent for each note sold.
The general revision of postmasters' salaries and allowances will be made as soon as possible, but as there are over 12,000 offices to be considered, it will take some time to complete the work. The salaries and rent allowances will be revised first, and each postmaster will be duly notified of any increase that he may be entitled to. The revision of allowances for forward and night duty will follow immediately after that of salaries.
All increases, either in salaries or allowances, will take effect from April 1, 1907.

I have here a cheque given in payment of the salary of the postmaster at Makaroff in Manitoba. The other information which I have in connection with this case was furnished me by the member for Dauphin, who, unfortunately, is not here to-night. The postmaster there, according to my information and according to a cheque which I have here, receives from the government a very small salary. His duties consist of attending to the arrival of the mail on the train at 11 o'clock at night and 4 in the morning the year round. He also attends to the distribution of the mail. For that he is paid one dollar per annum.
As mail courier probably.

They pay him quarterly in more senses than one, and I have here a cheque of 25 cents in payment of his salary for the quarter ending December, 1905, as postmaster at Makaroff station. He presented this cheque in the usual course, the bank charged him on each cheque 25 cents so the government can figure out what his annual recompense is.

I said a moment ago that the minimum salary paid to postmasters throughout Canada is $35. Sometimes we are asked to establish a temporary post office, perhaps for a club of business men at a summer camp, and to oblige them so that they will not be deprived of their mail, we appoint a postmaster, generally the caretaker, but of course we do not expect to pay him. As to the small payment to mail courriers our policy is to call for tenders and to give the mail contract to the lowest tenderer, but even when the amount is very low, we always find some one ready to offer his services at a lower figure. In the county of Nicolet which I represented for two sessions, there is a place, St. Gr^goire, where the service for years between that point and Nicolet, three or five miles, has been carried at 99 cents a year. The reason

is that the mail carrier also operates a stage and as the people know he must be at the station at certain times to deliver the mail, he gets practically all the patronage of the whole district, and while he receives only 99 cents as courier, he makes $600 or $700 on account of his privilege of carrying His Majesty's mail. This is a very old cheque, January, 1906.
Are not your government cheques payable at par at any bank?
Certainly.

The bank returned it to him. I may explain that Makaroff is a purely country post office on the Canadian Northern road. It could not possibly be for the purpose of business men, because there are very few business men there permanently. I am informed there are 23 farmers, at a minimum, using the post office the year round.

According to the last report of the department the revenue of Makaroff, in the county of Marquette, is $98.88, and we pay a salary of $87.83. We pay the postmaster besides $12 a year for office allowances.
Makaroff is in the local constituency of Dauphin.
Since 1906 many of these little villages on the Canadian Northern have grown into towns or cities.

I would like to call the attention of the Postmaster General to the needs of the people of North Toronto, a large and populous town contiguous to the city, for a letter carrier delivery. Until recently the town of West Toronto, which i3 now a portion of the city, had a letter carrier delivery, so also had the town of East Toronto. These two towns have now gone into the city, and are the district of the hon. member for North Toronto. The people of North Toronto think now that inasmuch as they are contiguous to the city they ought also to have a letter carrier delivery like West Toronto and East Toronto had before. I wish the minister would look into that and see if he cannot give this large town of 4,000 or 6,000 people a letter carrier delivery.
Do they elect aldermen?

Yes, it has a regular municipal organization, with a mayor and council. While I am on my feei, I would like to direct the attention of the minister to another matter, and that is a postal service for the new mining camp of Gowganda. The most active centre of business in all Canada to-day is in Elk lake and Gowganda. The minister has been good enough to give a service to Elk lake, and also I believe to South Gowganda. But Gowganda proper, which is now being cre-

ated a town by the legislature of Ontario, has for weeks been trying to get a postal service. The minister says he has taken it up and he is waiting for it to be erected into a town by the legislature of Ontario. But in the meantime it is an immense business centre. There are some days a hundred teams of traffic on the road to Gowganda. There are three banks now, there are hotels and stores being built every day, many capitalists are going up there, a telephone wire is being put in, and the people greatly feel the need of improved postal facilities. It is true it will cost a little more money, perhaps $5 or $10 a day, to establish a first-class courier service from Earlton and Elk lake, but there is so great a business there that it would pay the government to make an extra effort to give them a first-class accommodation. The revenue the customs house is taking in from the consumption of dutiable goods in Gowganda and in that northern country, I fancy, is larger than the revenue derived from cities of 20,000 persons. It is the centre of a great industry, and in view of these facts the government ought to follow the enterprise of those people and give them an excellent postal service. If the minister does that he will gain the approval not only of that portion of Ontario but of the whole country. There are men coming in there now from New York, from Montreal, from Toronto, from the old country, they are driving in there, they are on the trail now, for navigation to open to get in, and there will be a rush there in a short time' That being the case the place is worthy of a good postal service. I understand the minister has delayed action until the Ontario government has established the town site. But there are lots of houses there which would be glad to take care of the post office and give every reasonable accommodation.

I am glad my hon. friend has again brought this matter to my attention. As he is aware, we have called for tenders between Earlton and Elk City. Although during the season of bad roads we are paying $25 a day and for the remainder of the year $5 a day to the present service, yet the department has not hesitated for a moment to undertake that expense for the benefit of the people at Gowganda. At another point I have just established a tri-weekly service which is quite sufficient for the present. We are now paying $30 a day for only a few people in that country, but as soon as the tenders are in and the Ontario government have settled where the town site will be, the postal service will be established. But I do not think it would be fair to the Ontario government if we were to locate a post office outside the town site, I think it is only fair that we should wait the action of that government. The Ontario government are doing their utmost to meet our wishes.
I think the town site was defined yesterday in a Bill in the legislature.

I would like to say a word with reference to a free mail delivery for the town of Owen Sound. I forwarded a communication to the minister, but he has not yet answered it. The town of Owen Sound, as the minister may have noticed, is about to be incorporated into a city. It has a population at present of about 13,000, and it has lately annexed a portion of the adjoining village of Brooke. According to the last report of the Postmaster General, it had a revenue in 1908 of $23,000; and I think I am safe in saying that after the annexation of the town of Brooke it will have a revenue of $25,000 or $26,000. The number of post office orders issued last year was 3,116.
My hon. friend need not go any further. If they have that population and revenue they are entitled to free mail delivery within the city.
Thank you very much. Will the Postmaster General kindly inform me what steps are necessary to secure free mail delivery?

The city clerk sends officially to the department a statement as to the population of the new city of Owen Sound, because, I understand, you have made additions to the city. Then the city must undertake to number the streets in order to facilitate the delivery of letters. When that is done we send our inspector to organize the delivery, we appoint letter carriers and we give notice to that effect to the citizens.
Will the minister kindly send me a communication to that effect?
Very well.

I understand that the hon. the Postmaster General this afternoon made a statement that some of the members on this side of the House had been abusing the franking privilege by sending prospectuses in connection with some enterprise in Gow-ganda through the mails. As a member from that northern part of the country and being engaged in the mining industry to a certain extent I felt that perhaps it was a reflection upon myself.
No, it is not the hon. gentleman.

I think the hon. gentleman surely then should have been as frank <in his statement as hon. gentlemen on this side of the House were with him, because they named the parties who were doing the franking. I feel that it is a reflection upon myself and I rise to say that I am not guilty of using the franking privilege in that way. But while I am on my feet I might just say
that I know whereof I speak, because, within a very few days of becoming a candidate for the House of Commons, I had the honour to be one of your humble servants in being the postmaster at a town in the district of Algoma, and I was astonished at the quantity of matter that was franked through that office, notwithstanding that it is only a small country office, under the frank of several gentlemen on the other side of the House. It was sent all over the constituency and it was nothing more or less than political literature. I think that some portraits of the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) were franked through my post office, and one person had the

I might say-gall to want to take one of these portraits of our honoured leader, and have it posted on my store window to show the good qualities of our worthy Prime Minister. Of course, I objected to that, but I just want to say that there was a great deal of franking done through that small office and judging from the amount of matter that went through that office I am sure it must have been sent through some of the larger offices in thti district by the ton weight.

I did not have in mind the hon. gentleman this afternoon when I referred to the use which had been made of the franking privilege to spread broadcast circulars concerning Gowganda shares. What I said was that I had received from a firm in Toronto a complaint that a gentleman in the House, a new member probably, was using his frank to send circulars through the country. The firm which complained was in the same business as the member who was using the frank and it was a matter of rivalry between the two firms.

As I have the honour to represent the constituency in which Gowganda is situated, and since the minister has been good enough to clear the hon. member for Algoma (Mr. Smyth) of the charge made this afternoon, I would ask him to say that I am not the person referred to either. I have not abused the franking privileges in any way, nor shall I do so as long as I am a member of this House. I thank the hon. member for South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) for impressing upon the Postmaster General the advisability of giving postal facilities to Gowganda just as quickly as he possibly can. I would have said something before this upon the subject, had I not had the assurance of the Postmaster General that he was doing all he could and that he would have a postoffice there within a very few days.
My hon. friend was not the member mentioned nor intended to be mentioned. Therefore he is not guilty.

I would like to bring to the attention of the hon. the Postmaster

General the fact that the city of Sydney, in the constituency which I have the honour to represent, has a population, as nearly as it could be enumerated a year ago, by the clergymen of the different denominations, the school teachers in the city, and the assessors under the direction of the city council, of 14,800 plus and that for the last two or three years the question of free mail delivery has been mooted down there. Some three years ago the city numbered the different streets in order to comply with that part of the regulations. I would like to ask the Postmaster General now what further steps are necessary to be taken in order to have the free mail delivery system inaugurated in that city. Whilst I am on my feet there are three other little matters which I desire to mention. I am sorry to be delaying the passing of these estimates, I have no objection to them, I may say, and I feel quite satisfied the Postmaster General is endeavouring to do his very best under the circumstances. I am not criticising the expenditure. There is a new town called Waterford and at this place two coal mines were opened up about 15 months ago. There are residing at that place over 200 families, and as the mine goes deeper and its development and output increase this population wjll grow. A year from the incoming spring they will have anywhere from 500 to 600 men employed at mines Nos. 12 and 14. For the last eight or nine months mail matter directed to that place has been carried to the employees and people living there in the houses erected by the Coal Co. by merchants who truck their goods from Sydney, and the adjoining towns of Glace Bay and Dominion.
A post office was promised to Waterford and several local people were told they would be appointed postmaster, so that the Postmaster General will have no difficulty in selecting somebody for the position. It is absolutely necessary that a post office should be opened there when we consider that there are over 200 families who are dependent on the present altogether inadequate mail service. Then again, there is a stretch of twelve miles of rich farming country along the Myra river extending from Marion bridge to Salmon river, which is without a post office. There is a post office at Marion bridge and another at Salmon river but in the twelve miles between there i3 none, and in view of the fact that the Post Office Department had a surplus last year and that the estimates for this year include an increase of $193,000 for the mail service, I press upon the Postmaster General that he should open a new post office within that twelve miles of country. I would also direct the attention of the Postmaster General to another matter. If the hon. minister was present when the resolution of the hon. member for Guysbor-ough was being discussed early in the Mr. MADDIN.
session, he will remember that I pointed out that it would greatly assist the isolated fishing villages round the coast if they were granted better postal facilities. The constituency I represent has an extensive coast line and so my constituents are greatly interested in this matter. The mail for Bauline is made up at Main-a-Dieu and despatched to Bauline once every week on Friday. Now, the mail for Little Lorraine is also made up at Main-a-Dieu and goes to Little Lorraine three times a week. Little Lorraine and Bauline are equi-distant from Main-a-Dieu where the mail is made up and the mail carrier in going from Main-a-Dieu to Little Lorraine is obliged to pass within a mile or a mile and a half of Bauline, so that the Postmaster General could very easily provide that the people of Bauline should have a mail delivery three times a week. These people are all settled very closely together in a little cove thrust out on the Rocky shores of the Atlantic, and although they are only thirty miles from Sydney, so far as the mail service is concerned they are as far away from that city as if they lived in Vancouver.- These are the only matters in connection with the Post Office estimates which I wish to bring to the attention of the Postmaster General, and I trust he will give them the consideration which I think they deserve. As to free mail delivery in the city of Sydney, the Postmaster General has stated that if there was a population of over 13,000 in a city it was entitled to this privilege.
And a revenue of over $20,000. I am told that the revenue of Sydney is $22,000 so that it comes within the rule.
Yes. I may take it for granted then that the free mail delivery system will be extended to the town of Sydney.

My answer to the hon. gentleman from North Grey (Mr. Middle-bro) covers the city of Sydney. If there are over 200 families at Waterford I am surprised they have not already applied for a post office. How far are they from the nearest post office?

The nearest post office is at Lingan, five miles away. The Postmaster at Lingan has a son who runs a store at Waterford and he goes home nearly every day or his brother comes over to Lingan and the mail is handled by them in that way. I know for a fact that a request for a post office at Waterford was submitted to Mr. Johnston who represented this riding in the last parliament and he gave his personal pledge that a post office would be established. In fact this young man Burke, the son of the postmaster at Lingan who does business at the new town

of Waterford was promised the appointment of postmaster and so far as I am personally concerned there would be no objection to his appointment because he is doing his work pretty well now.
I will look up the papers in these cases.
1). TAYLOR. We would like very much to have the post office at New Westminster made a city post office. What are the requirements for a city post office?

There are three grades, the ordinary post office, the city staff post office, and finally the city post office. The New Westminster post office has not yet reached the dignity of city staff standing. New Westminster is entitled to free delivery and that will lead to the other grade in a few months probably. The other day we wrote to the New Westminster authorities and within five or six weeks we will probably have a free city delivery, but my hon. friend must not be too ambitious to begin with. We are chary about establishing city post offices because they will come under the Civil Service Act and that will entail quite a large expenditure, so that the revenue from such offices must be correspondingly large. It is only the post offices in Toronto, Montreal, Winnipeg, Vancouver, London, Hamilton, Quebec, Halifax and such large cities that are city post offices.
I appreciate very much what the Postmaster General is going to do in giving us free city delivery, but I would impress on him that the business of the New Westminster post office is very congested.
What is the revenue?
$22,000 according to the last report.
There are offices yielding a revenue of $60,000 which have not reached the dignity of city post offices, but that will come in time.

What we want in New Westminster is that the government shall take the responsibility of administering the office and provide a sufficient staff to do the work. At present the postmaster controls the office and pays his assistants, and he claims that the revenue does not permit him to engage sufficient men to provide the service to which the city is entitled; because, in addition to attending to the city service, the office is the distributing office for the district. The people of New Westminster will be very much disappointed to know that they are only getting half measure from the department, because they supposed that when they got free delivery, they would get what usually goes with it. I may say that New Westminster has been growing very rapidly of late. Within a few years its population has doubled, and the conditions which were all right a few years ago have become almost intolerable, and it will be a source of great embarrassment to the people if the post office does not keep up with the march of progress made by the city.

I would like to draw the attention of the minister to the fact that about a month ago I made application for a post office at Hazel Ridge, on the Molson cut-off of the Canadian Pacific Railway, about twenty-five miles east of Winnipeg. There is a station there, so that the expense wouljd be very small. At present people have to travel five miles to get their mail, and sometimes the roads are impassable. I hope the minister will see his way to provide that post office.
If the petition has been sent, it is probably now in the hands of the inspector, and I am awaiting his report.

I hope the report will be favourable. If not, I hope the minister will see it is made favourable. I have also sent a letter to the minister in regard to the need of improved mail facilities between Selkirk and Winnipeg.
I received the letter this morning, and the hon. member will get the answer to-morrow.
The Selkirk people are labouring under great disadvantages at the present time, and I trust that the minister will see his way to giving them the improved facilities they desire.

I want to say a *word in support of the position taken by my hon. friend from New Westminster. I never could understand why a postmaster in a city office and the men employed under him should not be directly employed and paid by the government. In offices where this is not the case, the tendency is to in crease the salary of the postmaster and get inefficient labour at small salaries to assist him.

The policy of the department, since a year or fifteen months ago, has been, wherever we are justified by the revenue of the post office, to fix the salary of the postmaster at a point and pay the officers under him.
Is there a fixed revenue ?
We have adopted the $20,000, but if the revenue is close to that' figure, we do not exact the pound of flesh. At the same time, we give the city the benefit of free delivery.

My point is that if you employ a postmaster to supervise
17X1

an office, with a revenue of $20,000, why do you not do the same for an office with a revenue of $15,000? I think the postmaster should be put on salary, and the employees under him should be paid and supervised by the department in both cases.

Complaints are made that the accommodation for the post office of the town of Pincher Creek, where I live, are very inadequate. It is a little place six feet by ten to accommodate a town of 1,500 people; that is the exact size, because I measured it, and there is only one wicket for all the business of the office. However I have no complaint to make about the way the business is conducted, including money orders and postal notes. I am sure the Postmaster General himself will admit that this is not the kind of mail service that should be given to the people of a town of that size. About a month ago I put in an application for a post office at Spring Ridge, which is in the direction of the Kootenay river. Has the minister arrived at a decision in regard to it ? I think generally we should have better mail service in that country than we have. I believe we are entitled to tri-weekly mails where now they are only weekly. There are mail routes there that have been established for ten or twelve years, well settled throughout their whole length and yet with only one mail a week. The people are complaining, more particularly in view of the fact that the Postmaster General is able to report a large surplus. One other point : complaints have been made to the Postmaster General, either through myself or direct, of the condition of the post office at' Macleod. I am sure that the Postmaster General will admit that the accommodations there are not sufficient. Macleod is an important centre of commerce. The post office service there is not fit for a place one-fifth the size, and the Postmaster General knows it. There are other complaints that I need not mention here.

As to the Macleod post office, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Herron) has already called my attention to the matter outside this House, and it is now engaging the attention of the department. This is the first time my hon. friend has told me of the unsatisfactory accommodation of the post office at Pincher Creek.
I was not complaining of the postmaster

I quite understand, it is a question of the accommodation. I take a special note of the hon. gentleman's complaint. I suppose he is simply re-echoing the complaint of the public, and we will notify the postmaster to provide the necessary accommodation. As regards the increase in the mail service from weekly to tri-weekly and daily, I may say that we have been making these increases quite Mr. RALPH SMITH.
freely for the last few years. In this year's report of the department, the hon. gentleman will see_ that the number of miles which the mails have been carried by railway, water route and ordinary land route was 1,129,779 miles more than the previous year. Of course, the railway and water routes account for a great deal of this, but still there is a large increase in the land route system also. I do not at all refuse to increase the service when there is the least justification for doing so. I have stated before, when my estimates were before the House, that where there is a population of, say, 25 or 30 people in the Northwest, I never refuse to open a post office. When the distance is not extraordinarily long I usually begin with a tri-weekly service. That is my policy for the west, and when the railways run near by and settlements extend, I increase the mails in many cases for tri-weekly to daily.

I have in mind now a route running south from my town through thickly-settled country for twenty miles or more, a route that has been in existence for ten years or more, and still only one mail a week. That is one case, and I believe you can find dozens of others in my own constituency. I do not know whether these people have been making requests for a better service-they have not been making them through me. But the facts are as I have stated. There are three or four hundred families on a route, and they come twelve miles for their mail to the different post offices along the route. I do not think that is a proper service.
I do not, either.

Has the minister any recent communications from the letter carriers of Victoria requesting to be placed on the regular Civil Service staff? I had occasion to discuss that question with them at some length when in Victoria, and it seemed to me the argument they made was a very good one indeed. They claimed that the care they are required to take in connection with the registered mail required just as much education, and just as much attention to duty and just as much responsibility as is required of many of the second and third-class clerks in the regular Civil Service. I would bespeak from the minister favourable consideration of this request, and I would ask him to tell me if he has come to any conclusion on the matter or whether it is still under consideration.

My hon. friend (Mr. Barnard) was absent from the House a moment ago when that matter was discussed. I explained my position. Briefly, I stated that a report is being prepared by the acting deputy Postmaster General, Mr. Laschinger, which I am submitting to coun-

cil. In fact, the question is before the government and is engaging the serious attention of my colleagues. More than that I cannot say, except that the letter carriers and the outside service generally know where my sympathies are.

I would like to ask the Postmaster General with regard to a petition I presented to him about a year ago, asking for a post office at Graham station. So far I have not had any word from the department though I have been led to believe that a report was made.
I will take that up to morrow. I have been away.

It is rather late now, and I feel ashamed to retard the passage of these estimates. But with regard to franking I wish to say a word. I may inform hon. gentlemen opposite that nothing of that kind was done in Kings and Albert. Our postage cost us between $500 or $600. I wish, however, to call the attention of the Postmaster General and hon. members on both sides of the House to a little matter . that may or may not be of importance. We have a large number of postmasters in Kings and Albert, and I am safe in saying that three-quarters of them are Conservatives. That is all right-

Hear, hear.
Mr. McALISTER

so long as they behave themselves. We paid for our postage, and I am sorry to inform the House that in certain localities a considerable quantity of campaign literature was not distributed by the postmasters and never reached its destination. I think the minister in those cases should take some action. I can produce men to whom papers were addressed who never received them, and these postmasters protested because their attention was called to the non-delivery. To hear hon. gentlemen opposite talking to-day one would suppose that everything that went wrong occurred on this side of the House.
Hear, hear.
I do not think that is the case; I think we are fairly equally divided in that respect.

Has a post office yet been opened in Pope, on the Grand Trunk Pacific? Up to two weeks ago.it had not been opened. The minister informed me that he was waiting for the recommendation of a postmaster. Many people there have to go several miles for their mail although there is a tri-weekly train service through the place, all because the defeated candidate who has the patronage has been careless or apathetic in making a recommendation. The people have petitioned for an office, naming a postmaster. This system of appointment should be amended and after a certain length of time, if the person controlling the patronage does not act the department should act on the petition of the people.

I will see that the appointment is made as soon as possible. My hon. friend will understand that in matters of this kind we have to act on the recommendation of some one in the constituency, and the candidate is, of course, a respectable man in good standing whose advice is likely to be valuable. I shall have the appointment made as soon as possible.
Mail services, $193,000.
Would the minister explain the system of rural free mail delivery which he has established?

I have already explained to the House during the last session the plan I would favour for the Dominion as regards rural mail delivery. I then said that I would not favour the system adopted generally in the United States because it was beyond our means. Without taking too much time to quote the figures of the American postal authorities, I may say there are two systems of delivery in the United States of mail matter addressed to persons residing in rural districts; first the rural free delivery and second the star route system which we have adopted. The former is widely known and need not be described particularly. The latter is incidental to the transportation of the mail over star or stage routes. The contracts for it include an obligation to deliver mail into boxes erected along the lines of such routes. Rural mail delivery as they have it in the United States to-day has been in operation for over 12 years. Starting as an experiment in 1895, on 93 rural routes, the number of routes increased in 1896 to 148, in 1899 to 391, in 1900 to 1,276, and from that on by leaps and bounds until at the close of the fiscal year June 30, 1908, there were 39,277 routes in operation. The expenditure-and this is the future which justified the department in adopting the present very conservative system of rural mail delivery- the expenditure for rural mail delivery in the United States, which in 1897 was only $J4,-840, in 1898 $50,241, in 1899 $150,012, and in 1900 $420,433, had at the close of the fiscal year June 30, 1908, reached the stupendous total of $34,360,463. It is out of the question for Canada, having the same territory with the climate she has-and of course the climate affects the routes-for the small population compared with the population of the United States and with a much smaller postal revenue to adopt the system which cost the United States annually $34,360,463.
Does the minister think that the United States pretend to furnish the mails in the sparsely settled districts of that country by the free mail delivery system?

Suppose the United States do not deliver the mail free in the sparsely settled districts, then if it costs so much money in the settled districts, what will it cost in our own districts where we have the same territory to cover? Listen to this:
The average annual salary paid to a rural carrier for the year ending June 30, 1893, was something over $178; for the year 1899, over $383; for the year 1901, over $406; for the year 1903, $532; for the year 1905, $650. In 1907 the rural mail carrier in the United States received an average salary of $711 a year, and for the year 1908, $877.88, and the end is not yet in sight.
Say the postal authorities of the United States. So it is out of the question for us to adopt the system of the United States. It would mean the ruin of the Post Office Department; it would mean wiping out of our total revenue. Now, we have adopted a system which is fairly described in this booklet which I intend to distribute to the members of the House. The Post Office Department has decided to undertake the delivery and collection of mail matter to a number of persons residing in rural districts along and contiguous to the line of travel of our existing stage routes, of one mile and upwards in length, upon receipt of a properly signed petition for such services from the residents of each of the rural districts traversed by such routes. Petition forms will be obtained upon application to the post office inspectors, or to the Post Office Department, mail contract branch, Ottawa. Now, who are the persons entitled to the privilege of a rural box? I cannot give a better definition of the system than by reading what the department is spreading through the country.
Perhaps the minister will allow this one item to stand over and pass the other two. I fancy this discussion will take an hour or two, there are several gentlemen who wish to speak on it.

I would prefer to pass the whole item. Supplementary estimates for this year will be laid on the table shortly, and the whole question can be resumed then. In these estimates which will be laid on the table within five or six days I have a similar item, not so large, under which this same discussion could take place. We need this money in the department. This discussion can take place at any time on the other items; in fact, T will arrange with my hon. friend the whip (Mr. Geo. Taylor) to have the discussion then.

I think that will be satisfactory.
Miscellaneous, $545,500.
My hon. friend from Yale-Cariboo (Mr. Burrell) wanted to say something about miscellaneous in the next item.

The very same items will come up in the supplementary estimates, but for lesser amounts, and I will arrange with my hon. friend the whip for a special debate. When these supplementary estimates are before the House all these questions may be brought up then.
I was going to ask the minister if he could not hold over this item till next week as I have to go away and may possibly be absent for several days.
I will not take up the supplementary items until my hon. friend gets back.
I would suggest that that pamphlet on rural mail delivery be distributed to each member.

Certainly.
Some resolutions reported.
